results.text:
Read text file `.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md`.
1|---
2|name: muse-round
3|description: Run one Muse Spark round on the MobileMoE-S decode kernels as a swarm. Explorers map the code and measurements into a shared analysis; then competing builders write and grade fused Metal kernels for the top inefficiencies. Both phases are tracked in shared documents.
4|---
5|
6|# One Muse Spark round: a swarm explores, then builds
7|
8|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed on main and tagged `muse-code-era` before the first Muse Code session; each later version is committed before the round that uses it. [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
9|
10|**Skill version 3.** This file, the role cards and tracking.md are versioned together; [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) lists every version. Each round records the version it ran (see *Versions* in tracking.md).
11|
12|You are Muse Spark, the **lead** of a Muse Code session in your own worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. `claude/muse-agent-brief.md` fixes the task, the four slots, the tools and limits, the grader command and the pass criteria (G1, G2). Two ADRs change it in four ways:
13|
14|1. **Harness** ([ADR 0006](../../../claude/adr/0006-muse-spark-in-muse-code.md)). You are a Muse Code session, not a Claude Code one. Muse Code adds no trailer, so you write it on every commit yourself (see *Commits*).
15|2. **No attempt limit and no stop rule** (ADR 0006). You decide when a slot is done. Every graded attempt is committed, so the history shows every try.
16|3. **A swarm** ([ADR 0007](../../../claude/adr/0007-muse-spark-swarm.md)). Helpers explore and build; you coordinate and commit.
17|4. **Files** (ADR 0007). `muse-spark/exploration/` and `muse-spark/implementation/` hold the round's shared documents, and they replace `strategy.md`. Kernels and `summary.md` stay where the brief puts them.
18|
19|The rest of the brief stands. The goal is unchanged: kernels that pass G1 and G2 and beat the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 rows, faster because they remove a cause you can name.
20|
21|## The swarm
22|
23|| Role | Name | Task | Card |
24||---|---|---|---|
25|| **Lead** (you) | | Start the helpers, keep the two READMEs, settle clashes, commit | this file |
26|| **Explorer** | `explorer-<territory>` | Map one territory into entries, and find where it loses time | [explorer.md](explorer.md) |
27|| **Verifier** | `verifier` | Check every inefficiency against its sources | [verifier.md](verifier.md) |
28|| **Builder** | `builder-<n>-<letter>` | Write and grade one solution for one hypothesis: one attempt | [builder.md](builder.md) |
29|| **Boundary agent** | `boundary-<n>` | Write what a hypothesis's solution must keep identical, and check passing attempts against it | [boundary.md](boundary.md) |
30|
31|You don't explore, build or grade yourself. Start each helper with a prompt of this shape:
32|
33|> You are `<name>`, a `<role>` in this round's swarm. Read `.agents/skills/muse-round/<card>` and `.agents/skills/muse-round/tracking.md`, then: `<task>`.
34|
35|[tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the shared documents (the two phase folders, their READMEs, entries and logs) and the rules every agent keeps. Read it before starting anyone. Up to 12 agents run at once, you included.
36|
37|**A checkpoint** is what you do each time a helper returns, and whenever the log shows something to settle:
38|1. **Read the log.** Read the phase log since your last checkpoint.
39|2. **Settle clashes.** When two entries describe one cause, keep the fuller one and set the other's status to `superseded by <entry>`. When two helpers work on one item, redirect one of them (`subagent_send_message`). Log what you decided.
40|3. **Refresh the tracker.** Update the phase README's tracker table, and raise the version of each hypothesis entry that changed.
41|4. **Raise the version.** Raise the phase README to its next version, and add its line to `## Versions`, naming the entries that changed and their versions (see *Versions* in tracking.md).
42|5. **Commit** the phase folder, plus any attempt that came back, as that version (see *Commits*).
43|
44|## The round
45|
46|### 0. Find where you are
47|
48|- Run `git log --oneline main -1`, then `git log --oneline --grep '^Muse Spark:' muse-code-era..HEAD`, which lists your earlier commits.
49|- **Round number:** `claude/findings/muse-round-<N>.md` holds Claude's measurement of round N, run after merging your branch. This round is one more than the highest N. With no such file, it is round 1.
50|- From round 2 on, read the newest of those files first. It has the G3 results of your attempts, and it is the first evidence for this round. The phase folders already exist:
51|  - explorers add a `## Round N` section to their entries rather than starting over;
52|  - you start explorers only for the territories the G3 results reopen;
53|  - the logs carry on.
54|- Read the brief.
55|
56|Done when you can name the round number, your committed attempts per slot, and the latest G3 results, if any.
57|
58|### 1. Exploration
59|
60|1. **Set up the folder.** Write `muse-spark/exploration/README.md` with a heading, its version line (v1, with skill version 3), the tracker (one row per territory) and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`. From round 2 on, the README carries on from its last version.
61|2. **Start the explorers and the verifier,** all at once, with these starting territories:
62|
63|   | Territory | Covers |
64|   |---|---|
65|   | `model` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py`: the decoder layer, `MoE.__call__` and everything around the slots |
66|   | `switch-layers` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/switch_layers.py`: the routed experts' path, `gather_qmm`, the sort from 16 rows |
67|   | `quantized-kernels` | `quantized.h` and `quantized_utils.h` in `.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/`: the `affine_gather_*` kernels behind `gather_qmm` |
68|   | `other-kernels` | the other Metal kernels in the same folder that the routing and combine slots launch: sort, softmax, reductions, elementwise, copies |
69|   | `vllm-metal` | `third_party/vllm-metal/vllm_metal/`: how the engine runs a decode step around the model |
70|   | `grader` | `bench/grader/`: the slot interface, what G1, G2 and the piece timing measure, and so the boundary every solution keeps |
71|   | `findings` | `claude/findings/` and `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/` |
72|   | `runs` | `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/`, `2026-10-29-baseline/` and `2026-10-30-micro/` |
73|
74|3. **Refocus as costs show up.** When an entry shows that one file holds most of a territory's cost, split it off as a territory of its own, with its own explorer. Merge or close a territory that turns out to hold nothing, and add one when an inefficiency points somewhere no one covers. Log each change and update the tracker.
75|4. **Checkpoint** each time a helper returns.
76|
77|**Done** when every territory entry is `done`, the verifier has returned, and every inefficiency is `confirmed`, `refuted` or `superseded`.
78|
79|### 2. The analysis
80|
81|Write the final `muse-spark/exploration/README.md`. It is the round's report on the code, for this round's builders and for future improvements:
82|
83|- **Tracker:** the final table.
84|- **Context:** the decode step, the MoE block and its slots, and what the measurements say about where the time goes.
85|- **Territory map:** how the territories feed each other. For each territory: what it receives, what it passes on, and its measured cost.
86|- **Inefficiencies, ranked:**
87|  - the confirmed ones inside the slots, ranked by predicted saving as a share of the decode step, averaged over 1, 8 and 32 rows;
88|  - each with its cost, kind and entry;
89|  - Claude's findings marked as Claude's, and the swarm's own reading marked as yours.
90|- **Recommendations:** the confirmed inefficiencies outside the slots, with their evidence. They're for surucuonur's team.
91|- **Refuted claims,** in one line each, so no one chases them again.
92|- **Files read:** links to each territory entry's list.
93|
94|From round 2 on, add a `## Round N` section: what the G3 results confirm, contradict or reveal.
95|
96|Commit it. **Done** when every ranked item links a confirmed entry and every number in the README has its source.
97|
98|### 3. Implementation
99|
100|Take the ranked inefficiencies in order, at most two at a time, in different slots so their attempts never touch. Write `muse-spark/implementation/README.md` with a heading, its version line, the tracker and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`. For each hypothesis:
101|
102|1. **Open the hypothesis.** Write `muse-spark/implementation/hyp-<n>-<slug>.md`, with status `boundary`, the inefficiency and the slot. Add its tracker row and log it.
103|2. **Draw its boundary.** Start `boundary-<n>` to write the boundary, and wait for it.
104|3. **Compete.**
105|   - Set the status to `building`.
106|   - Start 2 or 3 builders, `builder-<n>-a`, `-b` and `-c`. Give each a different direction drawn from the analysis: for example, fusing kernels, reading each weight byte once, or a different threadgroup shape.
107|4. **Collect.** Each time a builder returns:
108|   - checkpoint, committing its attempt folder with the hypothesis entry, the README and the log;
109|   - if the attempt passed G2, start `boundary-<n>` to check it.
110|5. **Harden.**
111|   - Pick the best attempt: it passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, and it is the fastest against the compiled reference across the three row counts.
112|   - Set the status to `hardening`, and start a builder for that attempt's next single change.
113|   - Repeat while the attempt still has a cause you can name and remove.
114|6. **Close.**
115|   - **`ready`:** the best attempt passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, and beats the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and you can name no further change worth making. Write the **Decision**: the attempt, why it is best, and what G3 should show.
116|   - **`dropped`:** say why.
117|
118|Then open the next-ranked inefficiency. **Done** when no confirmed inefficiency is left that you judge will pay. Write why in the implementation README.
119|
120|### 4. Finish
121|
122|1. **The implementation README:** the final tracker, one paragraph per hypothesis, and a **Ready to test** section. It names the attempt per slot that goes to G3, and the change in decode step period you expect at 1, 8 and 32 requests, with how you worked it out.
123|2. **The exploration README:** add *What building taught*, the analysis corrected by what the attempts showed.
124|3. **`muse-spark/summary.md`:** add a `## Round N` section with:
125|   - the skill version this round ran, and the final versions of both READMEs;
126|   - the final attempt per slot;
127|   - the number of graded attempts per slot, this round and in total;
128|   - the expected G3 change;
129|   - what you'd try next;
130|   - your recommendations outside the slots.
131|4. **Commit,** then reply with this round's commits and the words "Round N finished".
132|
133|## Your own rules
134|
135|- **Writes:**
136|  - you write the two READMEs, the hypothesis entries' status blocks and decisions, and `summary.md`;
137|  - every helper writes only what its card names;
138|  - all of it stays in `muse-spark/`, and a commit outside it is refused.
139|- **G3 and vLLM belong to surucuonur's team,** who run them after merging your branch.
140|- **The rules every agent keeps** are in tracking.md.
141|
142|## Commits
143|
144|You are the only agent that commits. Commit only on `muse-agent`.
145|- **What to add:** the phase folders that exist so far (only `exploration` until implementation starts) and the attempt folders that came back. An attempt another builder is still writing waits for its own commit. An entry that is mid-edit is committed as it stands, and finished in a later commit.
146|- **The message:**
147|  - a checkpoint's subject is `Muse Spark: <phase> v<N>: <what changed>`, the version it records;
148|  - other commits start with `Muse Spark:`;
149|  - every message ends with this exact trailer.
150|
151|```bash
152|git add muse-spark/exploration muse-spark/implementation muse-spark/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>
153|git commit -m "Muse Spark: implementation v4: experts attempt 3 graded, passes G2" \
154|  -m "Co-Authored-By: Muse Spark (Meta Model API) <muse-spark@meta-model-api.invalid>"
155|```
156|
157|Use no other co-author. The hooks refuse a commit without this trailer, a commit outside `muse-spark/`, and any merge. Push, merge, rebase, git config and hook skipping stay with surucuonur.

Read text file `.agents/skills/muse-round/tracking.md`.
1|# The swarm's shared documents, and the rules every agent keeps
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Part of the [muse-round skill](SKILL.md). [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|Every agent of the round reads this file. The documents below are how the swarm shares what it knows and how surucuonur follows the round while it runs, so keep them current as you work, not at the end.
6|
7|## The two phase folders
8|
9|| Folder | Phase | Holds |
10||---|---|---|
11|| `muse-spark/exploration/` | Exploration | the analysis: `README.md`, territory and inefficiency entries, `log.md` |
12|| `muse-spark/implementation/` | Implementation | the report: `README.md`, hypothesis entries, `log.md` |
13|
14|Kernels stay where the grader reads them: `muse-spark/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>/`.
15|
16|Each folder has three kinds of document:
17|
18|- **`README.md`.** The phase's document. Only the lead writes it, refreshing it and raising its version at every checkpoint. It opens with its version line and the tracker table below.
19|- **Entries.** One file per territory, inefficiency or hypothesis. The owner keeps it current, and other agents append notes.
20|- **`log.md`.** One line per event, from every agent, appended only.
21|
22|## Versions
23|
24|Every shared document carries a version number, so a reader knows which version they're looking at, and git holds every version.
25|
26|**Phase versions.** Each README opens with its version line:
27|
28|```markdown
29|**Version:** v5 · 2026-11-04T09:40Z · skill version 3
30|```
31|
32|- **Who raises it:** the lead, at every checkpoint, and each version is exactly one commit.
33|- **The commit:** its subject names the version, `Muse Spark: exploration v5: <what changed>`. `git log --grep 'exploration v5:'` finds it, and `git diff` between two such commits shows what changed.
34|- **The changelog:** the README ends with `## Versions`, one line per version, newest first, naming the entries that changed and their new versions:
35|
36|```markdown
37|- v5 · 2026-11-04T09:40Z · split quantized-kernels in two · changed: territory-quantized-kernels v4, ineff-quantized-kernels-2 v2
38|```
39|
40|**Entry versions.** Each entry's status block has a `Version` line, starting at 1:
41|- **Territory and inefficiency entries:** the owner raises it with every change to its own text. The verifier raises it when it writes the verdict.
42|- **Hypothesis entries:** the lead raises it at each checkpoint where the entry changed, builders' and the boundary agent's sections included.
43|- **Notes:** a note under `## From other agents` leaves the version alone. The owner raises it when folding the note in.
44|
45|## The README trackers
46|
47|Exploration, `exploration/README.md`:
48|
49|| Territory | Agent | Status | Inefficiencies | Updated |
50||---|---|---|---|---|
51|| `quantized-kernels` | `explorer-quantized-kernels` | exploring | `ineff-quantized-kernels-1` (confirmed), `-2` (open) | 2026-11-04 09:40Z |
52|
53|Implementation, `implementation/README.md`:
54|
55|| Hypothesis | Slot | Builders | Attempts: G1, G2, µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (compiled) | Status |
56||---|---|---|---|---|
57|| `hyp-1-fused-gather` | `experts` | `builder-1-a`, `builder-1-b` | 3: pass, pass, 41 / 55 / 180 (48 / 70 / 260) | hardening |
58|
59|## Entries
60|
61|Each entry opens with a status block that its owner keeps current:
62|
63|```markdown
64|- **Owner:** explorer-quantized-kernels
65|- **Status:** exploring
66|- **Version:** 3
67|- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T09:40Z
68|- **Next:** read the 32-row dispatch of affine_gather_qmm
69|```
70|
71|Entries are named so that two agents never pick the same name:
72|- `exploration/territory-<territory>.md`
73|- `exploration/ineff-<territory>-<n>.md`, numbered by the explorer of that territory
74|- `implementation/hyp-<n>-<slug>.md`, numbered by the lead
75|
76|**Another agent's entry:** append under its `## From other agents` heading, starting with your name and the time. The owner's text stays as written, so two agents never overwrite each other. The owner reads these notes and folds in what holds.
77|
78|### Territory entry
79|
80|1. Status block (statuses: `exploring`, `done`).
81|2. **What it does** in the decode step, in a few lines.
82|3. **The checklist** below, filled in for each piece of code or table in the territory.
83|4. **Relations:** which territories feed it and which it feeds, with the data passed.
84|5. **Inefficiencies:** links to the entries this territory raised.
85|6. **Files read**, and what each one gave.
86|
87|### Inefficiency entry
88|
89|1. Status block. The statuses are `open`, `confirmed`, `refuted` and `superseded by <entry>`; only the verifier sets `confirmed` or `refuted`.
90|2. **Slot:** `routing`, `combine`, `experts`, or `outside the slots`.
91|3. **What happens:** what the code does, and where (file and lines).
92|4. **Cost** at 1, 8 and 32 rows: kernels × the fixed cost per kernel, bytes ÷ peak bandwidth, and the measured time with the table it comes from.
93|5. **Kind:** overhead-bound, bandwidth-bound or compute-bound, in the terms of `claude/GLOSSARY.md`.
94|6. **Spans:** the territories involved.
95|7. **Predicted saving** if removed, in µs per decode step at 1, 8 and 32 rows, with the arithmetic.
96|8. **Verdict**, written by the verifier: each claim checked, and the result.
97|
98|### Hypothesis entry
99|
100|1. Status block. The lead owns it; the statuses are `boundary`, `building`, `hardening`, `ready` and `dropped`.
101|2. **Inefficiency** it removes, and the slot.
102|3. **Boundary**, written by the boundary agent: what the solution must keep identical (see `boundary.md`).
103|4. **One section per builder:** its direction, its attempts (folder, predicted and measured µs per layer at 1, 8 and 32 rows, G1, G2), and what each attempt taught.
104|5. **Boundary checks** of the attempts that passed G2.
105|6. **Decision:** the best attempt and why. When the status is `ready`, it states what G3 should show.
106|
107|## The checklist
108|
109|Fill it in for each piece of code you inspect, so that no piece is judged without its neighbours:
110|
111|- **Callers:** who calls it, and with what shapes at 1, 8 and 32 rows.
112|- **Callees:** what it calls, down to the Metal kernel it launches.
113|- **Data:** each input and output with shape, dtype and layout. Where it is produced, and where it is consumed next.
114|- **Neighbours:** what runs just before and after it in the decode step, and what a replacement must keep identical.
115|- **Cost:** the kernels it launches, the bytes it reads and writes (weight bytes counted per read), and its measured time with the table the time comes from.
116|- **Invariants:** what correctness depends on: the G2 tolerances, the tie rule for the 4th and 5th expert, the bfloat16 rounding points.
117|
118|## The log
119|
120|Append one line per event with the shell, so lines from several agents never mix:
121|
122|```bash
123|printf '%s | %s | %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "explorer-quantized-kernels" "posted ineff-quantized-kernels-2: each weight byte read 4 times at 32 rows" >> muse-spark/exploration/log.md
124|```
125|
126|Log when you start, claim something, post or confirm an entry, change direction (what from, what to, and which entry made you), grade an attempt (with its verdict), and finish.
127|
128|## Adapting to the others' work
129|
130|Before every new piece of work, and after every post:
131|1. Read the phase README's tracker and the newest 30 lines of the phase log (`tail -n 30`).
132|2. Then change direction when:
133|   - **someone else covers it:** another entry already covers the same code or cause, so append to that entry instead of starting a second one;
134|   - **its premise fell:** the claim your work rests on was refuted;
135|   - **something pays more:** an open item in your territory or task predicts a larger saving than what you're on, and nobody owns it.
136|3. When you change direction, log it with the reason, and write it in your own entry's status block.
137|
138|Two claims on the same item go to the lead, who settles them.
139|
140|## Rules for every agent
141|
142|- **Writes go only to `muse-spark/`, in the files your role names.** Everything else in the worktree, and everything outside it, is read-only.
143|- **Only the lead commits.** Helpers never run `git add` or `git commit`.
144|- **The grader is the only GPU job.** Run it only as a builder, through the brief's command; it waits its turn when another run has the GPU. Load no model and start no other GPU work: the machine has 16 GB and slows down sharply when memory runs short.
145|- **Every number has a source:** a file and line, a table (path and row), a grader verdict (attempt folder), or arithmetic shown in full.
146|- **Credentials stay unread:** `.env` files, `~/.config/muse/` and any key store.
147|- **The API-stage kernels** in the history before the tag `agent-era` are from an earlier, removed stage (PROVENANCE.md) and stay unread.

Read text file `.agents/skills/muse-round/explorer.md`.
1|# Explorer
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Part of the [muse-round skill](SKILL.md). [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are `explorer-<territory>`, one of the swarm's explorers. You map one **territory** of the code or the measurements, and you find where it loses time. The lead's prompt names your territory and its paths. [tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the documents you write and the rules you keep.
6|
7|First read:
8|- the brief, `claude/muse-agent-brief.md`: *The task*, *The slots* and *How each attempt is judged*;
9|- `claude/GLOSSARY.md`;
10|- the exploration README's tracker, so you know who covers what.
11|
12|## Steps
13|
14|1. **Open your entry.** Write `muse-spark/exploration/territory-<territory>.md` with its status block (`exploring`), and log that you started.
15|2. **Map the territory.** For each piece of code or table in it, fill in the checklist in your entry, with a source for every line.
16|   - Follow a call or a buffer into a neighbouring territory as far as you need to understand your own piece. Leave what you learn there as a note in that territory's entry. The swarm sees the whole system only when each explorer sees the edges of its own territory.
17|3. **Post inefficiencies.** Each time you find time lost, write an inefficiency entry with its cost arithmetic and predicted saving, and log it. Examples:
18|   - kernels that could be one;
19|   - weight bytes read more than once;
20|   - threads left idle;
21|   - work repeated across layers or rows.
22|4. **Adapt.** After every post, follow *Adapting to the others' work* in tracking.md. Narrow in on the part of your territory where the measured cost is; when the cause lies in another territory, put a note in that territory's entry instead of exploring it yourself.
23|5. **Answer notes.** Read the notes under `## From other agents` in your entries, and fold in what holds.
24|
25|**Done** when every piece of code or table in your territory has its checklist filled with sources, every inefficiency you found has an entry, and every note on your entries is answered. Then set your entry to `done`, log it, and return the names of your entries with one line each.
26|
27|## Sources outside the worktree
28|
29|MLX's C++ code, which picks the kernel and its threadgroup sizes for each op, isn't installed; only the Metal headers are. If web fetch works, read it at the installed version (`.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; print(mx.__version__)"`) in `github.com/ml-explore/mlx`, and cite the URL with the tag and lines.
30|
31|## What you write
32|
33|Your territory entry, your inefficiency entries, notes in other entries, and log lines.

Read text file `.agents/skills/muse-round/verifier.md`.
1|# Verifier
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Part of the [muse-round skill](SKILL.md). [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are `verifier`. The implementation phase builds only on inefficiencies you confirmed, so every claim an inefficiency rests on is checked against its source before anyone builds on it. [tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the documents and the rules.
6|
7|## Steps
8|
9|Repeat until done:
10|
11|1. **Find open entries:** `grep -l 'Status:\*\* open' muse-spark/exploration/ineff-*.md`.
12|2. **Check each claim** the cost and the predicted saving rest on:
13|   - open the cited file at the cited lines;
14|   - find the cited table row;
15|   - redo the arithmetic.
16|3. **Write the entry's `Verdict` section.** Mark each claim `confirmed`, `wrong` (with what is right, and its source) or `no source`.

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write a faster MobileMoE-S decode kernel
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
12|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
13|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
14|
15|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
16|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
17|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
18|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
19|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
20|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
21|
22|## The slots
23|
24|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the step: 1 to 32 in decode. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
25|
26|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
27|
28|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
29|
30|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
31||---|---|---|---|
32|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
33|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
34|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
35|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
36|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
37|
38|Reference:
39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
69|
70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
93|
94|## Tools and limits
95|
96|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
97|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
98|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes; stop one that hangs.

100|

104|
105|- **Write only inside `muse-spark/`.** Never change `bench/`, `claude/`, `results/`, `tools/`, `third_party/`, or any other file. A copy of the grader you edit is never used.

1|# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.
6|
7|## Hardware limits
8|
9|**Peak bandwidth**:
10|The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
11|_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed
12|
13|**Peak compute**:
14|The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
15|_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)
16|
17|**Achieved bandwidth**:
18|The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
19|_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)
20|
21|**Arithmetic intensity**:
22|Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
23|_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio
24|
25|**Ridge point**:
26|The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.
27|
28|**Roofline**:
29|The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.
30|
31|## Bottlenecks and fixes
32|
33|**Bandwidth-bound**:
34|A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.
35|
36|**Compute-bound**:
37|A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.
38|
39|**Overhead-bound**:
40|A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
41|_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)
42|
43|**Bottleneck**:
44|The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
45|_Avoid_: issue, slowness
46|
47|**Kernel**:
48|One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
49|_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)
50|
51|**Occupancy**:
52|The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
53|_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)
54|
55|**Knock-out**:
56|A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
57|_Avoid_: ablation
58|
59|**Baseline**:
60|The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.
61|
62|**Fix**:
63|One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
64|_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak
65|
66|## Inference
67|
68|**Prefill**:
69|Processing a request's whole prompt in one pass before any token is generated.
70|
71|**Decode step**:
72|One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.
73|
74|**Decode rows**:
75|The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
76|_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency
77|
78|**Client concurrency**:
79|The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.
80|_Avoid_: batch size
81|
82|## Mixture of experts
83|
84|**Expert**:
85|One of the interchangeable feed-forward blocks in a layer; MobileMoE-S has 60 routed experts per layer.
86|
87|**Active experts**:
88|The experts the router picks for one token in one layer (4 for MobileMoE-S).
89|_Avoid_: selected experts, top-k experts
90|
91|**Distinct experts**:
92|The number of different experts used by all decode rows together in one layer during one decode step; it decides how much expert weight data the step must read.
93|_Avoid_: unique experts, expert coverage
94|
95|## Models
96|
97|**MobileMoE-S**:
98|Meta's smallest on-device mixture-of-experts model (about 1.3B parameters in total, about 272M used per token), studied here in its SFT (full-precision) and QAT (int4) variants.
99|
100|**Muse Spark**:
101|Meta's hosted model. In this project it chooses which pieces of the decode step to replace and writes their kernels, working in its own Muse Spark session; it is never the model under study.
102|
103|**Muse Code**:
104|Meta's own coding agent for the terminal, built on Muse Spark; the only program in which Muse Spark does its work in this project.
105|_Avoid_: Muse CLI, Meta Code
106|
107|**Muse Spark session**:
108|A Muse Code session in which Muse Spark writes every turn, the lead's and every helper's, kept apart from Claude's work by its own branch, folder and commit trailer.
109|_Avoid_: guardrail (for the session itself), Meta mode
110|
111|## Muse Spark's work
112|
113|**Slot**:
114|One replaceable piece of the mixture-of-experts block (routing, combine, or the routed experts), with fixed inputs and outputs, that Muse Spark may replace with its own kernels.
115|_Avoid_: target (that is a slot Muse Spark has chosen), module
116|
117|**Round**:
118|One Muse Spark session in which a swarm explores and then builds, followed by Claude's independent measurement of what it produced.
119|_Avoid_: iteration, cycle
120|
121|**Swarm**:
122|All the agents of one round, the lead and its helpers, working toward one goal through shared documents that each of them reads and adds to.
123|_Avoid_: team, crew
124|
125|**Lead agent**:
126|The one agent of a swarm that starts the helpers, keeps the shared documents current, settles clashes and commits; it neither explores nor grades.
127|_Avoid_: orchestrator, main agent
128|
129|**Helper agent**:
130|An agent the lead starts: an explorer, the verifier, a builder or a boundary agent. It reports back and never commits.
131|_Avoid_: worker, subagent (when the role matters, not the mechanism)
132|
133|**Reminder agent**:
134|One of Muse Code's own background agents, which watch the lead's progress and may nudge it, for example to check a claim before it says it is done; Muse Spark writes their turns too, but they take no part in the work.
135|_Avoid_: helper (that is one the lead starts)
136|
137|**Exploration phase**:
138|The first part of a round, in which explorers map the code and the measurements and find where the decode step loses time.
139|
140|**Implementation phase**:
141|The second part of a round, in which builders write and grade solutions to the confirmed inefficiencies.
142|_Avoid_: hypothesis phase
143|
144|**Territory**:
145|The part of the code or the measurements that one explorer covers: a module, a single important file, or a measurement document.
146|_Avoid_: area, lens
147|
148|**Analysis**:
149|The swarm's shared account of the code, written during exploration: the context, how the territories feed each other, and the ranked inefficiencies, each with its cost and sources.
150|_Avoid_: diagnosis, findings (those are Claude's)
151|
152|**Inefficiency**:
153|One cause of lost time in the decode step: where it is in the code, what it costs, and what removing it should save. It is confirmed or refuted against its sources before anyone builds on it.
154|_Avoid_: issue, bottleneck (that is the single largest cause)
155|
156|**Hypothesis**:
157|A proposed solution to one inefficiency: the slot it replaces, the boundary it keeps and the saving it predicts, tested by competing attempts.
158|_Avoid_: strategy, plan
159|
160|**Boundary**:
161|What a solution must keep identical so that the steps before and after its slot work exactly as before: the slot's inputs and outputs, their dtypes, and the rounding points.
162|_Avoid_: interface (unqualified), contract
163|
164|**Attempt**:
165|A solution a builder has graded and the lead has committed; attempts for a slot are numbered in order and have no limit.
166|_Avoid_: try, submission, draft

`CompiledMLPBlocks` fuses a whole MoE/MLP block's elementwise glue with
`mx.compile` on decode-shaped calls (`third_party/vllm-metal/vllm_metal/compiled_mlp.py:174-196`).

(`compiled_mlp.py:115-131`): MobileMoE-S's MoE block is never wrapped, even
with `VLLM_METAL_COMPILED_MLP=1` (default off, `envs.py:121`). And
`MAX_COMPILED_TOKENS = 4` (`compiled_mlp.py:49`) would route 8/32-row steps
eager anyway. So on the benchmark model every layer runs routing (~12 kernels:

## What happens

vllm-metal has a GQA decode kernel that reads each KV head once for all

(`third_party/vllm-metal/vllm_metal/metal/ops_internal.h:47-54`). MobileMoE-S

`gqa_decode_geometry_supported` fails (`metal/paged_attention.cpp:67-76`) and
decode silently falls back to the per-token kernel: one threadgroup per
(query head, token) (`paged_attention.cpp:1026-1028`), each computing

29|   ~131 MB/step excess at 32 rows, inside the 908 MB.
30|4. At 1 row the grids are 24/24/48 threadgroups (~1.5-3K threads, ~5-10% of the

16|
17|From 14 rows up, MLX runs its quantized products split-K: the K dimension is cut
18|into chunks, each chunk writes its own float32 copy of the output
19|(`split_k × rows × outputs` numbers), and a second kernel reads them back and
20|adds them up (`quantized.cpp:1166-1226`, threshold `get_qmv_batch_limit` = 14 on

23|expert's gate/up/down; the buffers total 173 MB per step (23.6 + 15.7 + 15.7 +
24|23.6 + 31.5 + 31.5 + 31.5 MB). That is why the step writes 3 MB at 1 row and
25|20-21 MB at 8 rows but 251-266 MB at 32 rows (GPU counters, 2026-11-02, as
26|quoted in the findings).

13|weight-and-sum combine, and the shared expert. All 20 layers are MoE layers
14|(`interleave_moe_layer_step: 1` in
15|`models/MobileMoE-S-QAT-mlx-bfloat16/config.json`, `mobilemoe.py:240-244`).
16|Constants: D=768, E=60, K=4, H=384, routed_scaling_factor=2.5, norm_topk_prob=true,
17|int4 affine group_size=32, expert layout [E, in, out] (`transposed_experts: true`).

21|### A. `MoE.__call__`, router: cast + matmul + sigmoid (`mobilemoe.py:219`)
22|
23|- **Callers:** `DecoderLayer.__call__` (`mobilemoe.py:258`) with `x = post_attention_layernorm(h)`.
24|  Decode shapes (plain MLX): `x` [rows, 1, 768] bf16 — decode feeds [rows, 1] ids
25|  (`bench/micro/breakdown.py:442-460`, greedy keeps `[:, None]`), so at 1/8/32 rows:
26|  [1,1,768] / [8,1,768] / [32,1,768]. The slots flatten lead dims to [rows, 768]
27|  (`bench/grader/slots.py:107`).
28|- **Callees:** `x.astype(float32)` → AsType kernel; `self.router` (`nn.Linear(768, 60, bias=False)`,
29|  weight [60, 768] float32, `mobilemoe.py:197`) → Matmul kernel; `mx.sigmoid` → Sigmoid kernel.

31|  (`results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md:133`: AsType 20, Matmul 20, Sigmoid 20).

1|# Territory: quantized-kernels
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-quantized-kernels

8|
9|## What it does
10|
11|This territory is the `affine_gather_*` Metal kernels behind `mx.gather_qmm`
12|(`quantized.h`, `quantized_utils.h`). In MobileMoE-S decode they run the routed
13|experts' gate/up/down products: one `gather_qmm` each per layer per step, always
14|dispatched to `affine_gather_qvm` (proof below). 60 `GatherQMM` launches per step
15|at every row count (`results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md:152-154`).
16|
17|## The checklist
18|
19|### A. `affine_gather_qvm` + `qvm_impl` — the kernel decode actually runs
20|
21|- **Callers:** `GatherQMM::eval_gpu` in
22|  `github.com/ml-explore/mlx`, tag `v0.32.4`,
23|  `mlx/backend/metal/quantized.cpp:1980-2094`. MobileMoE calls
24|  `mx.gather_qmm(..., transpose=False, group_size=32, bits=4, mode="affine")`
25|  with `x` `[pairs,1,K]` so `M=1` (`third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:172-184`,
26|  `switch_layers.py:176-199`). Dispatch: `M==1 < vector_limit==4`
27|  (`quantized.cpp:2005,2034`) rules out `gather_qmm`; the rhs fast path needs
28|  `M==1 && B>=16 && right_sorted_ && B/E>=4` (`quantized.cpp:2012`) but
29|  `B/E = rows*4/60 <= 2.1` at `rows<=32` (needs `rows>=60`), so it never fires;
30|  `transpose_==false` selects `gather_qvm` (`quantized.cpp:2073-2093`).
31|  Shapes at 1/8/32 rows: gate/up `M=1,N=384,K=768,B=rows*4`; down
32|  `M=1,N=768,K=384,B=rows*4`.
33|- **Callees:** `gather_qvm` launches `affine_gather_qvm` (`quantized.h:2355-2416`,
34|  via `quantized.cpp:1461-1529`) with `group_dims=(32,2,1)=64` threads,
35|  `bn = min(group_size,32)*2 = 64`, grid `(M,(N+63)/64,B)`: gate/up
36|  `(1,6,B)`, down `(1,12,B)`. Each threadgroup runs `qvm_impl`
37|  (`quantized.h:1222-1330`): 2 simdgroups x 32 lanes; each lane owns one K
38|  element per iteration and decodes 32 outputs via `qouter`
39|  (`quantized.h:452-553`, bits=4 path `:503-509`).
40|- **Data:** `w` uint32 `[E,in,out/8]` (4-bit, 8 per word along out),
41|  `scales`/`biases` bfloat16 `[E,in,out/32]`, `x` bfloat16 `[B,1,K]`,
42|  `rhs_indices` uint32 `[B]`, `y` bfloat16 `[B,1,N]`; per-pair offsets via
43|  `adjust_matrix_offsets` (`quantized.h:1636-1688`). Weights/scales read
44|  exactly once per pair: gate pair traffic = 6 tiles x 64 lanes x 24 iters x
45|  16 B weights = 144 KB = `768*384/2` B, scales+biases 36 KB; `x` row re-read
46|  12x per pair per product (each of 6 tiles' 2 simdgroups streams the full row:
47|  `qvm_impl:1275-1287`), ~55 KB x per pair over gate+up+down vs 3.75 KB needed.
48|- **Neighbours:** before: router `inds` (model territory) + `_gather_sort` at
49|  `indices.size>=64` (switch-layers; sort buys only L2 locality since rhs never
50|  fires). Between gate/up and down: activation (other-kernels). After: combine
51|  (model). Replacement must keep G2: every element within 2 bfloat16 ulp of the
52|  reference (1e-3 floor), float32 accumulation, bfloat16 rounding points.
53|- **Cost:** 60 launches/step (~6 us each: routed experts 140 kernels/0.92 ms @1,
54|  `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md:179-185`). Bytes (GPU counters,
55|  `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md:17-18`): experts saves
56|  51 MB read in 0.92 ms @1 (55 GB/s), 908 MB in 14.67 ms @32 (62 GB/s, 31% of
57|  peak). Grids @1 row are 24/24/48 threadgroups (~1.5-3K threads, ~5-10% of
58|  slots; whole-step Compute Occupancy 9%, same table).
59|- **Invariants:** `w = scale*q + bias` per group of 32 along out; output column
60|  `o` in word `o/8` bits `4*(o%8)` (brief); float32 accumulate, bfloat16 store
61|  (`qvm_impl:1324-1329`); fully K/N-aligned launches (384/768 % 64 == 0,
62|  768/384 % 32 == 0), no tail waste.
63|
64|### B. `affine_gather_qmm_n` / `affine_gather_qmm_t` + `qmm_n_impl` / `qmm_t_impl` — never run in decode
65|
66|- **Callers:** only `GatherQMM::eval_gpu` when `M >= vector_limit`
67|  (`quantized.cpp:2034-2051`); decode has `M=1`. Documented so no one chases them.
68|- **Callees:** `affine_gather_qmm_n` (`quantized.h:2501-2568`) /
69|  `_t` (`:2418-2499`), `BM=BN=BK=32`, `QuantizedBlockLoader`
70|  (`quantized.h:665-791`) + `BlockMMA`, `gemm_loop_*` (`quantized_utils.h:6-90`).
71|- **Data / Neighbours / Cost / Invariants:** same dtypes and `scale*q+bias`
72|  decoding as (A); zero cost in decode.
73|
74|### C. `affine_gather_qmm_rhs` + `schedule_row_tile` — never run in decode
75|
76|- **Callers:** only when `M==1 && B>=16 && right_sorted_ && B/E>=4`
77|  (`quantized.cpp:2012-2032`); needs `rows>=60`, unreachable at `rows<=32`.
78|  This is the kernel that would batch same-expert pairs (offsets +
79|  `schedule_row_tile`, `utils.h:501-542`); its absence is why each pair keeps
80|  its own grid (see ineff-quantized-kernels-1).
81|- **Callees:** `affine_gather_qmm_rhs` (`quantized.h:2570-2718`), `BM=16,BN=32,
82|  BK=32`, same loader/MMA helpers as (B).
83|- **Data / Neighbours / Cost / Invariants:** same as (A); zero cost in decode.
84|  Note for switch-layers: model sorts at `>=16` rows but dispatch ignores
85|  sortedness below `B/E>=4`.
86|
87|### D. `affine_gather_qmv_fast` / `affine_gather_qmv` — never run in decode
88|
89|- **Callers:** only when `transpose_==true` and `M < vector_limit`
90|  (`quantized.cpp:2053-2071`); MobileMoE uses `transpose=False`.
91|- **Callees:** `qmv_fast_impl` (`quantized.h:850-962`) / `qmv_impl` (`:964-1123`)
92|  via `affine_gather_qmv_fast` (`:2231-2291`) / `affine_gather_qmv` (`:2293-2353`).
93|- **Data / Neighbours / Cost / Invariants:** non-transposed `[E,out,in]` layout
94|  only; zero cost in decode.
95|
96|### E. Shared helpers
97|
98|- `dequantize` (`quantized.h:557-663`), `qdot`/`qdot_safe` (`:221-450`),
99|  `load_vector`/`load_vector_safe` (`:28-219`): per-bit paths, bits=4 used.
100|- `QuantizedBlockLoader` (`:665-791`): dequantize-on-load into threadgroup
101|  memory; used by (B)/(C), not by (A).
102|- `adjust_matrix_offsets` gather variant (`:1636-1688`): per-threadgroup index
103|  lookup, negligible cost.
104|- `gemm_loop_aligned/unaligned/finalize` (`quantized_utils.h:6-90`): the
105|  K-loop for (B)/(C) only.

114|## Inefficiencies
115|
116|- `ineff-quantized-kernels-1` (open): per-pair qvm grids run expert traffic at

9|## What it does
10|
11|The routing and combine slots are built from MLX's generic Metal kernels, not the
12|quantized ones: a small matmul plus sigmoid for router scores, bias add, negate,
13|`argpartition` top-4, `take_along_axis` gather, row reductions, broadcast
14|multiply/divide, astype copies, and the final add. This territory maps those ops to
15|the kernels in `.venv/.../mlx/backend/metal/kernels/` (headers, installed) and the
16|launch choices in MLX's C++ dispatch (read at tag v0.32.4 on GitHub — installed
17|version confirmed 0.32.4), with shapes, bytes, and launch structure at 1, 8, 32 rows.

1|- **Owner:** explorer-vllm-metal
2|- **Status:** done
3|- **Version:** 2

5|- **Next:** none (checklist sourced; ineff-1/2 superseded into findings-1/runs-4, ineff-3/4 open)
6|
7|## What it does
8|
9|vllm-metal's model runner turns each decode step's scheduled requests into one
10|lazy MLX graph — decode rows first, then prefill rows — submits it with
11|`mx.async_eval`, and samples the next tokens. Around the model it owns: batch
12|assembly and paged-attention metadata, the per-layer patched attention path
13|(QKV prep, RoPE, fused cache write, paged-attention kernel), the decode
14|dispatch policy (compiled vs eager MLP/MoE blocks), selective lm_head
15|projection, and sampling (native greedy argmax or a torch-CPU bridge).
16|
17|## The checklist
18|
19|### 1. `execute_model` → `_start_paged_forward` (graph build + submit)
20|
21|- **Callers:** `MetalWorker.execute_model` (`v1/worker.py:315`), called by the
22|  vLLM engine once per step; on the paged path it returns `None` and the engine
23|  later calls `sample_tokens` (`v1/worker.py:328`).
24|- **Callees:** `_handle_new_requests`, `_collect_cached_requests`,
25|  `prepare_grouped` (attention metadata), `_target_forward` (the model),
26|  `_submit_paged_forward_outputs` → `mx.async_eval`
27|  (`v1/model_runner.py:3257-3376,1480-1800,891-900`).
28|- **Data:** in: `SchedulerOutput` (request ids, block tables, seq lens). Built:
29|  `input_ids` [1, rows] int32 (`model_runner.py:1654-1658`); `OffsetCache(0)`
30|  per layer; `cu_seqlens`. Out: `logits` [1, rows, vocab] (float, vocab 256k?
31|  — MobileMoE vocab; see model territory), stashed in `_PagedForwardState`.
32|- **Neighbours:** before: scheduler (`schedule`, 0.06/0.12/0.30 ms at 1/8/32
33|  rows) and the decode-pipeline gate (`begin_step`). After: `sample_tokens` →
34|  `_sample_paged_batch`. A replacement must keep the packed [decode][prefill]
35|  row order and `logits_cu_seqlens` indexing the sampler uses.
36|- **Cost:** runner work outside the model 0.5/0.9/1.6 ms per step at 1/8/32
37|  rows; graph record 2.41/2.45/3.12 ms; encode 4.10/4.70/6.46 ms
38|  (`claude/findings/step-breakdown.md` §2 table). No kernels of its own except
39|  one `AsType` on the inputs (step-breakdown §4 table).
40|- **Invariants:** pure-decode steps keep the model's own `__call__` and packed
41|  boundaries (no selective-logits gather); the pipeline gate guarantees a
42|  deferred step's membership can only shrink (`decode_pipeline.py:237-249`).
43|
44|### 2. `_sample_paged_batch` + `DecodePipeline` (sampling)
45|
46|- **Callers:** `sample_tokens` after `execute_model` returned `None`
47|  (`v1/model_runner.py:3398-3450`); or the deferred path
48|  `_submit_deferred_decode_sample` on pipeline-eligible steps.
49|- **Callees:** greedy: `SamplingBatch.native_decode_tokens` → `mx.argmax`
50|  (1 kernel) (`v1/sampling_batch.py:221,644-649`); else `mx.eval` + `mlx_to_torch`
51|  (fp32 cast) + vLLM torch sampler on CPU (`sampling_batch.py:651-663`).
52|- **Data:** in: `logits` [1, rows, vocab]; out: one token id per row (+ optional
53|  logprobs). The deferred path feeds lazy tokens as next step's `input_ids` via
54|  device gather, no host round-trip (`decode_pipeline.py:287-324`).
55|- **Neighbours:** after the forward's `async_eval`; before scheduler output
56|  processing. G2's end-to-end check (same 24 greedy tokens) pins this path.
57|- **Cost:** sampling + bookkeeping 0.10/0.13/0.20 ms CPU at 1/8/32 rows; the
58|  native-greedy sample is one argmax kernel (step-breakdown §2; benchmark
59|  workload is greedy so the torch bridge never runs there).
60|- **Invariants:** native greedy requires temp≈0, no top-k/p, no penalties, no
61|  logprobs (`sampling_batch.py:173-194`); seeded/non-greedy stays on torch.
62|
63|### 3. Patched attention path per layer (`sdpa_forward`)
64|
65|- **Callers:** the model's attention layers, wrapped by `patch_sdpa_attention`
66|  at load (`attention/impls/sdpa_wrapper.py:258-286`, `runtime/sdpa.py:128-133`).
67|  MobileMoE-S (12 q heads / 4 kv heads) takes the SDPA runtime.
68|- **Callees:** `prepare_sdpa_qkv` (q/k/v projections, q/k norms, RoPE) →
69|  `queries[0]` gathers + `astype` + `mx.contiguous` → fused `reshape_and_cache`
70|  kernel → `paged_attention_primitive` → o_proj
71|  (`attention/impls/sdpa.py:669-679,722-724`, cache write ~`:800-815`,
72|  attention dispatch ~`:830+`).
73|- **Data:** q/k/v [1, L, heads, 64] bfloat16 → contiguous [L, heads, 64] cache
74|  dtype; slot_mapping/block_tables/seq_lens metadata memoized per forward
75|  (`_kernel_metadata`); KV cache [blocks, 16, 4, 64] bfloat16.
76|- **Neighbours:** between post-norm... actually input_norm → attention → residual
77|  add → post_norm → MoE. Must keep: RoPE positions per request, cache-write
78|  visibility to the read in the same step (graph provenance on the aliased
79|  cache buffers), output dtype = query dtype.
80|- **Cost:** vLLM attention vs plain MLX: 320 vs 220 kernels/step (+60 Gather,
81|  +60 Contiguous from 2 rows up; cache write 20 fused vs 40); knock-out
82|  7.48 vs 5.60 ms at 32 rows, of which the kernel is 4.33 vs 3.12 ms and the
83|  copies 0.24 ms; record CPU 1,716 vs 1,062 µs (step-breakdown §3-4).
84|- **Invariants:** G2 pins greedy tokens end to end; attention numerics must
85|  match MLX SDPA within that.
86|
87|### 4. Paged-attention decode kernel selection (GQA miss)
88|
89|- **Callers:** `sdpa_forward` via `ops.paged_attention_primitive` → C++
90|  dispatch `paged_attention.cpp`.
91|- **Callees:** GQA decode kernel only if
92|  `gqa_decode_geometry_supported` admits the layout
93|  (`metal/ops_internal.h:47-54`, `metal/paged_attention.cpp:67-76,156`);
94|  MobileMoE-S 12/4/64/16 is not among the six listed layouts, so decode uses
95|  the per-token kernel (one threadgroup per query head × token,
96|  `paged_attention.cpp:1026-1028`), where each group reads its KV head via
97|  `head_idx / num_queries_per_kv` (`metal/kernels_v2/pagedattention.metal:859-860`).
98|- **Data:** reads each KV head 3× (once per sharing query head), partly from
99|  cache (decode-bottlenecks §6 table: 12/4 takes 2.3× the time of 4/4 for the
100|  same cache bytes).
101|- **Neighbours:** after `reshape_and_cache`, before o_proj. A GQA replacement
102|  must reproduce the per-token kernel's softmax numerics exactly enough for G2's
103|  token check.
104|- **Cost:** direct kernel timing at 32 rows: 125 µs/layer at 256-token ctx
105|  (vs 55 for 4/4), 569 µs at 1,152-token ctx (vs 247); 1-row: 26 vs 19 µs
106|  (decode-bottlenecks §6). In-step attention kernel knock-out: 4.33 ms at
107|  32×128 (step-breakdown §3).
108|- **Invariants:** none beyond G2 tokens; nothing logs the fallback today.
109|
110|### 5. Compiled-MLP decode dispatch (`CompiledMLPBlocks`)
111|
112|- **Callers:** `ModelLifecycle.install_decode_dispatch` after load+split
113|  (`v1/model_lifecycle.py:228-239`), via `load_model`
114|  (`v1/model_runner.py:714`). Gated by `VLLM_METAL_COMPILED_MLP` (default
115|  **False**, `envs.py:121,170`); skipped for pooling and LoRA serves.
116|- **Callees:** wraps target blocks so decode-shaped calls
117|  (`x` [1, ≤4, D], fp16/bf16) run `mx.compile(inner.__call__)`
118|  (`compiled_mlp.py:174-196`).
119|- **Data:** unchanged shapes/dtypes; the trace captures load-final weights.
120|- **Neighbours:** wraps whole MoE/MLP blocks; the MoE block's shared expert
121|  compiles as part of the outer trace. Must keep bit-identical outputs on the
122|  quantized path (pinned by tests/parity harness per the module docstring).
123|- **Cost:** `_target_policies` lists only Qwen3Next/Qwen3.5 block types
124|  (`compiled_mlp.py:115-131`) — MobileMoE-S's MoE block is **not wrapped** even
125|  with the flag on, so its routing (240 kernels/step) + combine (100/step) run
126|  fully eager: knock-out 1.02 + 0.61 ms at 1 row, 1.68 + 0.33 ms at 32 rows

219|- **Boundary floor — traffic the slots mandate** (unremovable within the
220|  interface, so it caps every saving): per layer, experts must write
221|  y [rows,4,768] bf16 (rows×6144 B) and combine must re-read it; routing must
222|  write inds+weights [rows,4] (rows×32 B) for experts/combine to read. Per step
223|  @32 rows: y 196 KB × 2 (write+read) × 20 layers = 7.9 MB → 0.04 ms at
224|  200 GB/s; inds/weights ≈ 41 KB → negligible. Saving floor ≈ 0.04 ms @32 rows
225|  (≈ 0.001 ms @1 row): fusing *within* slots captures essentially all of each
226|  slot's cost; cross-slot fusion is not expressible (`routing+combine` still
227|  runs the reference experts + shared expert between the parts, brief:171).
228|- **Piece timing vs G3 (builder warning):** the piece timing medians 30 repeats
229|  of 20-layer evals per part and sums the parts; G3 medians 3 full steps. A
230|  candidate can win the piece timing yet lose G3 (e.g. via cache/overlap effects
231|  the isolated evals don't see). The gap must exceed the repeat spread.

1|# Territory: findings
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-findings
4|- **Status:** done
5|- **Version:** 4
6|- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T22:05Z
7|- **Next:** done — lead to settle overlaps; verifier to reconcile saving bases (findings-2 vs qkern-1) and the runs-3 premise
8|
9|## What it does
10|
11|This territory is the measured evidence, not code: the three findings documents in
12|`claude/findings/` and the raw breakdown run in
13|`results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/`. It tells every other explorer what each piece
14|of the decode step costs in place (kernels, CPU, knock-out savings) so no
15|inefficiency is claimed without a measured cost. The headline numbers the swarm
16|builds on: the 1-row step is a chain of 867 kernels where routing+combine cost
17|1.63 ms of 4.75 ms, and at 32 rows the routed experts cost 14.67 ms of 28.19 ms
18|while reading 908 MB against the 443 MB they need.
19|
20|## Checklist
21|
22|### A. Step periods and the vLLM-vs-plain-MLX gap
23|
24|- **Callers:** `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md` §1 (lines 101-116); the brief's
25|  slot costs (§`routing`/`combine`/`experts`) rest on these knock-outs.
26|- **Callees:** `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` "Step period by mode"
27|  (lines 14-24) and "Each repeat" (lines 26-52); raw records in `runs-plain.jsonl`,
28|  `runs-vllm.jsonl` (one record per run).
29|- **Data:** bare-mode medians of 3 repeats. Plain MLX: 4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms at
30|  1 / 8 / 32 rows × 128-token prompts, 33.20 ms at 32 × 1024. vLLM: 5.64 / 14.30 /
31|  30.47 / 39.71 ms. vLLM's extra: +19% / +7% / +8% / +20% (+6.51 ms long-context).
32|- **Neighbours:** piece B (runner spans) explains the 1-row gap as CPU; piece H
33|  (attention) explains the long-context gap. Replaces decode-bottlenecks finding 1
34|  ("5-10%"), which compared different harnesses.
35|- **Cost:** the whole-step denominators every saving is measured against: 4.75 ms
36|  at 1 row, 28.19 ms at 32 rows (plain MLX, bare).
37|- **Invariants:** steady decode steps only (first 5 of 256 dropped); random-token
38|  prompts, different generators per engine (routing differs slightly: 40.1 vs 36.4
39|  distinct experts/layer at 32 rows); machine paged heavily throughout (Limits,
40|  step-breakdown lines 493-497; `machine-*.txt`).
41|
42|### B. Runner spans: who sets the pace, CPU or GPU
43|
44|- **Callers:** step-breakdown §2 (lines 117-144); decode-bottlenecks §4
45|  (lines 135-156) for the profiled submit-call split.
46|- **Callees:** tables.md "Time per step in each runner span, cpu mode" (lines 54-71)
47|  and "CPU time per step to build each piece's graph" (lines 73-110).
48|- **Data:** per-step means over 3 repeats, cpu mode. vLLM schedule: 0.06 / 0.12 /
49|  0.30 / 0.48 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 / 32-long. Encode (`submit`): plain 2.61 / 3.61 /
50|  6.02 ms, vLLM 4.10 / 4.70 / 6.46 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows. GPU-wait inside
51|  `mx.async_eval`: 0.41 ms (vLLM, 1 row) vs 19.39 ms (vLLM, 32 rows).
52|- **Neighbours:** at 8+ rows the GPU sets the pace (runner work is free); at 1 row
53|  vLLM is CPU-set (0.41 ms GPU wait; plain MLX has 0.67 ms wait, GPU-set with CPU
54|  to spare). 1-row vLLM cpu-mode column is an upper bound (instrumentation
55|  lengthens the step 5.64 -> 7.44 ms).
56|- **Cost:** scheduler never the problem (0.06-0.30 ms); runner outside the model
57|  0.5 / 0.9 / 1.6 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows; encoding the largest CPU cost (4.10 ms
58|  vLLM vs 2.61 ms plain at 1 row).
59|- **Invariants:** cpu-mode 1-row vLLM figures are upper bounds; profiled Python
60|  figures (decode-bottlenecks §4) overstate Python parts.
61|
62|### C. Per-piece cost at 1 row: routing+combine beat the expert math
63|
64|- **Callers:** step-breakdown §3 "With one request" (lines 155-195);
65|  bottleneck-explained §3 (lines 106-118); brief slot costs (routing 1.02 ms,
66|  combine 0.61 ms, experts 0.92 ms at 1 row).
67|- **Callees:** tables.md knock-out tables (lines 320-356: "What removing a piece
68|  saves", median and fastest-repeat) and "Each piece at 1 row" (lines 358-375);
69|  kernel counts from tables.md "Kernel operations per step" (lines 112-147).
70|- **Data:** plain MLX, per step of 20 layers. Routing: 240 kernels, 173 µs CPU,
71|  saves 1.02 ms (4.3 µs/kernel). Routed experts: 140 kernels, 220 µs CPU, saves
72|  0.92 ms (6.6 µs/kernel). Combine: 100 kernels, 75 µs CPU, saves 0.61 ms
73|  (6.1 µs/kernel). Shared expert: 80 kernels, saves 0.51 ms. Output layer: 1
74|  kernel, saves 0.39 ms (158 GB/s). MoE all: 560 kernels, 2.94 ms. Attention all:
75|  220 kernels, 1.21 ms.
76|- **Neighbours:** vLLM 1-row knock-outs are ranges/noise (paging; step-breakdown
77|  lines 175-176) — use plain MLX at 1 row. Sync-mode GPU times are NOT used
78|  (sum 5-8x the real step; Limits lines 503-505); only kernel counts come from
79|  sync mode.
80|- **Cost:** routing+combine = 340 kernels and 1.63 ms, a third of the 4.75 ms
81|  step — more than the routed experts' 0.92 ms. Most pieces cost 4-7 µs/kernel.
82|- **Invariants:** knock-out saving = piece cost where it runs (CPU, GPU or both);
83|  a faster version gains less than the full saving (Limits lines 507-509).
84|
85|### D. Per-piece cost at 32 rows: the routed experts take half the step
86|
87|- **Callers:** step-breakdown §3 "With 32 requests" (lines 196-230);
88|  bottleneck-explained §4 (lines 120-133); brief (experts 14.67 ms of 28.19 ms).
89|- **Callees:** tables.md lines 320-356 (knock-outs) and 377-394 ("Each piece at
90|  32 rows"); both engines agree within 2.5% at 32 rows.
91|- **Data:** plain MLX, per step. Routed experts: 260 kernels (140 + 120 sort ops:
92|  60 Gather, 40 ArgSort, 20 FloorDivide — tables.md lines 136-139), 537 µs CPU,
93|  saves 14.67 ms (52%). Attention all: 5.60 ms (kernel 3.12). Shared expert: 2.90
94|  ms. Output layer: 2.50 ms. Routing: 1.68 ms. Combine: 0.33 ms. MoE all: 680
95|  kernels, 17.09 ms (60%).
96|- **Neighbours:** vLLM output layer saves 5.08 ms vs plain 2.50 ms — unexplained,
97|  not the kernel (`lm_head_shapes.txt`: 2.351 vs 2.356 ms either layout, same
98|  logits); at least one vLLM 32-row knock-out removes more than its piece
99|  (top-level savings sum to 33.3 ms > 30.3 ms step). Use plain MLX figures.
100|- **Cost:** experts 14.67 ms (52%); attention 5.60 ms (20%); routing bookkeeping
101|  stops mattering (6%).
102|- **Invariants:** 32-row savings are not additive (removing a large piece changes
103|  overlap; replayed outputs change later routing — step-breakdown lines 225,
104|  507-509).
105|
106|### E. Derived bandwidth/compute and the fixed cost per kernel
107|
108|- **Callers:** step-breakdown §3 "Memory bandwidth and compute, piece by piece"
109|  (lines 231-295); bottleneck-explained §§1-3 (lines 47-118); decode-bottlenecks
110|  §2 (lines 83-112).
111|- **Callees:** tables.md "Achieved bandwidth and compute of each piece" (lines
112|  408-438) and "The whole step's achieved bandwidth and compute" (lines 440-450);
113|  op mix from tables.md "Operations per step by type" (lines 149-159).
114|- **Data:** peaks 200 GB/s, 5.2 TFLOP/s. Whole step uses 12-19% of peak bandwidth
115|  (38 / 29 / 26 / 39 GB/s plain at 1 / 8 / 32 / 32-long), 5.1-8.7x its lower
116|  bound — overhead-bound in both engines. At 1 row a piece's GB/s follows bytes
117|  per kernel: output layer 158 (1 kernel, 61.6 MB), shared expert 86, projections
118|  ~30, routing 4 (240 kernels, 3.7 MB). Kernel count 867 (1 row) / 987 (32 rows)
119|  plain, 968 / 1088 vLLM; tiny-op chain 6.81 µs/op end to end.
120|- **Neighbours:** bytes count each weight once and skip activations, so derived
121|  GB/s are lower bounds on real traffic. GPU counters (runs territory,
122|  2026-11-02) check them: 1-row reads 193 MB vs 180 MB needed; output layer
123|  167 GB/s vs derived 158.
124|- **Cost:** at 5-7 µs/kernel, a kernel reading 0.37 MB cannot exceed 50-75 GB/s;
125|  at 1 row the limit is the kernel count, not bandwidth.
126|- **Invariants:** lower bound = max(bytes/200 GB/s, FLOP/5.2 TFLOP/s); 1-row vLLM
127|  excluded (CPU-set, savings are CPU time).
128|
129|### F. Expert bytes: per-pair reads, and the grouped kernel that never runs
130|
131|- **Callers:** bottleneck-explained §4 (lines 135-194); decode-bottlenecks §5
132|  (lines 158-204); step-breakdown §3 memory-traffic subsection.
133|- **Callees:** per-layer distinct experts in `runs-plain.jsonl` (`distinct_experts`
134|  in sync records; e.g. 43,50,45,...,39 at 32 rows, total 802 pairs; means in
135|  tables.md lines 396-406); MLX `quantized.cpp:2011-2012` rule (`M==1 && B>=16 &&
136|  sorted && B/E>=4` → grouped needs 240+ pairs = 60+ rows); `switch_layers.py:181`
137|  (sort from 64 pairs = 16 rows). Byte totals (908 MB read, 443 MB needed) are
138|  runs-territory counter data (2026-11-02) cited by the findings.
139|- **Data:** one expert = 3 × 294,912 int4 weights = 0.553 MB (weights 147,456 B +
140|  scales/offsets 36,864 B per matrix). 32 rows: 2,560 pairs ask 1,416 MB;
141|  distinct-once needs 443 MB; 908 MB reached memory → 465 MB extra (30% of the
142|  1,557 MB step reads), cache served the other half of the 973 MB repeat reads.
143|  Per-pair vs grouped on equal balanced data (chained 20 layers): 5.08→3.82
144|  (−25%, 8 rows), 8.12→5.65 (−30%, 16 rows), 15.02→9.63 ms (−36%, 32 rows).
145|  Weight layout within 4% for grouped — not the cause.
146|- **Neighbours:** real routing shares less than the test (3.2 pairs/expert at 32
147|  rows in the counted step, 128/40.1; 2.2 at 16 rows) — grouped gain there is
148|  untested. Sorting from 16 rows only reorders the per-pair kernel's visits.
149|- **Cost:** experts move 908 MB over 14.67 ms = 62 GB/s (31% of peak); 908 MB at
150|  peak = 4.5 ms, 443 MB at peak = 2.2 ms, yet measured 14.67 ms — most is kernel
151|  efficiency, not bytes (estimate).
152|- **Invariants:** random-token prompts; real text may route to a different
153|  distinct-expert count (bottleneck-explained "What remains uncertain").
154|
155|### G. Split-K partial writes from 14 rows up
156|
157|- **Callers:** bottleneck-explained §6 (lines 223-283); step-breakdown §3 memory
158|  traffic (writes) and §6 "new lead, not yet a fix" (lines 485-488).
159|- **Callees:** MLX `quantized.cpp:89-125` (`get_qmv_batch_limit` = 14 rows on
160|  applegpu_g13s), `:1166-1226` (split choice), `:1909-1915`; runs-territory
161|  counter data cited: writes 3 / 20-21 / 251-266 MB per step at 1 / 8 / 32 rows;
162|  knock-out write savings 57 MB (q,k,v) and 102 MB (shared expert).
163|- **Data:** split_k at 32 rows: q 12, k 24, v 24, o 12, shared gate/up 8, down 16;
164|  buffers split_k × rows × outputs × 4 B: q 1.18, k/v 0.79, o 1.18, shared 1.57
165|  MB per layer → 23.6 + 15.7 + 15.7 + 23.6 + 31.5 + 31.5 + 31.5 = 173 MB/step.
166|  No split-K for output layer (4,008 tiles), routed experts (batched kernel),
167|  router (not quantized).
168|- **Neighbours:** check sums — worked-out 55 MB vs measured 57 MB (q,k,v), 94 vs
169|  102 MB (shared); 4× the 8-row 20 MB + 173 MB ≈ 253 MB vs measured 251-266 MB.
170|  Each layer's buffer is 0.8-1.6 MB, so read-back may come mostly from cache.
171|- **Cost:** 173 MB written per step + read-back + 7 extra add kernels/layer (140
172|  per step). Time effect NOT measured — "a lead, not yet a fix".
173|- **Invariants:** needs a patched MLX to test (no setting turns split-K off);
174|  bfloat16 partials would change rounding.
175|
176|### H. Attention re-reads and the vLLM gap (for the attention territories)
177|
178|- **Callers:** bottleneck-explained §5 (lines 196-221); decode-bottlenecks §6
179|  (lines 206-237); step-breakdown §4 (lines 381-416).
180|- **Callees:** vllm-metal `metal/ops_internal.h:47-54` (GQA layout list misses
181|  MobileMoE-S 12/4/64/16), `paged_attention.cpp:67-76,156,1026-1028`,

183|  (`[0]` gathers + `Contiguous`); tables.md kernel/CPU/knock-out rows for

185|- **Data:** cache needed at 32 rows ≈ 160 MB (7,792 tokens × 1,024 B × 20 layers);
186|  plain MLX kernel reads 265 MB (1.7x, 85 GB/s over 3.12 ms); vLLM kernel 4.33 ms
187|  at 32×128, gap +6.51 ms at 32×1024 (estimate: triple reads). Direct-kernel test:
188|  12/4 takes 2.3x the 4/4 time for the same bytes (125 vs 55 µs @256 tokens/layer).
189|  vLLM attention path: ~1 ms Python/step vs 0.23 ms plain; +60 Gather, +60
190|  Contiguous (copying only from 2 rows up), +140-220 view ops; encode +1.1-1.5 ms.
191|- **Neighbours:** cause sits in attention/vllm-metal code — other explorers'

194|- **Cost:** attention in place: plain 1.21 / 5.60 ms, vLLM 2.0-2.6 / 7.48 ms at

198|### I. Repeated work: real but cheap
199|
200|- **Callers:** step-breakdown §5 (lines 417-466); tables.md "Work repeated in

213|- **Cost:** ≤0.2 ms/step; worth making as clean-ups, not speed-ups.
214|- **Invariants:** lhs_indices helps only below 16 rows (MLX uses sorted kernels

217|### J. Compiling the MoE block: −29% at 1 row
218|
219|- **Callers:** decode-bottlenecks §3 (lines 113-133); bottleneck-explained §8 fix-1
220|  row; step-breakdown §6 (fix 1 stays first).
221|- **Callees:** 2026-10-30-micro `moe_parts.py` data (runs territory) as quoted:

223|- **Data:** 6.02→4.27 ms (−29%) at 1 row; 6.95→5.61 (−19%) at 4; 14.03→13.45 (−4%)

228|  gain less. Fix 1 + fix 2 (projection fusion, −80-100 kernels ≈ −0.5 ms GPU,
229|  −0.25 ms CPU) + fix 3 (CPU trim) estimated 5.5 → 3.5-4 ms at 1 row.
230|- **Cost:** the 29% is the measured existence proof that fusing the MoE
231|  bookkeeping pays at 1 row.
232|- **Invariants:** test routing spread wider than the sweep (47.8 vs 38.2 distinct
233|  experts/layer at 32 rows); sync times don't add up to a step.

235|### K. Limits and caveats every claim inherits
236|
237|- **Callers:** step-breakdown Limits (lines 491-523); bottleneck-explained "What

## Context

A decode step produces one token per request. On plain MLX with 128-token prompts the bare step takes 4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (Claude: `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md:14-24`, via [territory-findings.md](territory-findings.md) §A); vLLM takes 5.64 / 14.30 / 30.47 ms. A step is 867 kernels at 1 row, 987 at 32 rows, and stays far below both hardware limits (whole-step 24–41 GB/s against 200 GB/s peak, ≤9% of peak compute), so it is overhead-bound throughout (Claude: step-breakdown §3, [territory-findings.md](territory-findings.md) §E). Each tiny kernel costs ~6.81 µs end to end (Claude: `results/runs/2026-10-30-micro/step_parts.txt`, via [territory-runs.md](territory-runs.md)).

The MoE block (`MoE.__call__`, `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:217-232`) runs in all 20 layers of every step ([territory-model.md](territory-model.md)). Per layer it launches: routing, 12 kernels (router cast+matmul+sigmoid, bias add, negate, argpartition, gather, weight norm); the routed experts, 7 kernels at 1 row (3 products + activation + 3 off-chain index ranges) and 13 from 16 rows (6 sort/unsort glue kernels); combine, 5 kernels (cast, multiply, sum, cast, add with the shared expert); plus the shared expert, 4 kernels. The three slots mirror this split: `routing` (240 kernels/step), `experts` (140–260/step), `combine` (100/step).

Where the time goes (Claude's knock-outs, plain MLX, via [territory-findings.md](territory-findings.md) §C–D and [territory-runs.md](territory-runs.md)): at 1 row, routing costs 1.02 ms and combine 0.61 ms — together 1.63 ms of the 4.75 ms step (34%), more than the routed experts' 0.92 ms. At 32 rows the experts cost 14.67 ms of 28.19 ms (52%) while routing falls to 1.68 ms (6%) and combine to 0.33 ms (1%). The experts read 908 MB at 32 rows against 443 MB for the distinct experts (Claude: `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`, via [territory-runs.md](territory-runs.md)) — half the bytes are repeat reads, and even so the 14.67 ms runs at only 62 GB/s (31% of peak), so most of it is kernel efficiency, not bytes (swarm reading: [ineff-findings-2.md](ineff-findings-2.md), [ineff-quantized-kernels-1.md](ineff-quantized-kernels-1.md)).

## Territory map

Measurements feed code: `runs` and `findings` map the raw tables and Claude's findings into the costs every inefficiency cites. `model` maps `MoE.__call__` and hands the experts path to `switch-layers`, the routing/combine chains to `other-kernels`, and the `gather_qmm` call to `quantized-kernels`. `vllm-metal` maps the engine around the model. `grader` maps the slot contract every solution keeps.

| `model` | `x` from post-attention norm; `h` for the residual | routing → `inds`/`weights`; experts → `y`; combine → `out` to next layer | routing 1.02/1.68 ms, experts 0.92/14.67 ms, combine 0.61/0.33 ms at 1/32 rows (knock-outs) |
| `switch-layers` | `x` [rows,1,768], `inds` [rows,1,4] from `MoE.__call__` | `y` in `inds` order to combine | experts path: 140 kernels/0.92 ms at 1 row, 260/14.67 ms at 32 rows |
| `quantized-kernels` | pairs + expert weights via `gather_qmm` | products to activation (gate/up) and unsort (down) | 60 GatherQMM launches/step; experts traffic at 55–62 GB/s (31% of peak) |
| `other-kernels` | ops from `MoE.__call__`; `y` from experts; weights; shared expert | `inds`/`weights` to experts/combine; `out` onward | routing chain 240 kernels, combine chain 100 kernels; every kernel far below occupancy |

## Inefficiencies, ranked

Confirmed inefficiencies inside the slots, ranked by predicted saving as a share of the decode step (plain MLX: 4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows), averaged over the three row counts. Shares shown as 1-row / 8-row / 32-row (mean). **The five `experts` entries are one combined fix: their savings do not add** (verifier reconciliation; joint ceiling 443 MB at streaming rate ≈ 11.5 ms at 32 rows). Each item names whether its evidence is Claude's measurement or the swarm's own reading.

1. **Per-pair qvm grids run expert traffic at ~1/3 peak** — 10.5 / 18.7 / 30.5% (mean 19.9%). Cost: 0.92 ms at 1 row, ~5.1 ms at 8 rows, 14.67 ms at 32 rows (62 GB/s, 31% of peak). Kind: overhead-bound. Entry: [ineff-model-2.md](ineff-model-2.md) (saves 0.47 / 0.30 / 0.19 ms fusing to 1 kernel/layer). Costs are Claude's knock-outs; the chain inventory, the 32-row overlap cap, and the launch-shape detail (128-thread `col_reduce_small`, cache-resident intermediates) are the swarm's own.

Kind: overhead-bound with a bandwidth-waste component. Entry: [ineff-runs-1.md](ineff-runs-1.md) (saves 0.0 / 0.6 / 2.3 ms: excess bytes at peak bandwidth, a floor). The op counts are Claude's tables; the proof that the sort cannot change kernel choice below 60 rows (so standalone removal loses time) is the swarm's own.
