## What it does

`SwitchGLU.__call__` (`third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/switch_layers.py:176-199`) runs the
routed experts of one MoE layer: it expands `x`, and from 16 rows up sorts the
(token, expert) pairs by expert (`_gather_sort`), runs the three expert products
(up, gate, down) through one `mx.gather_qmm` each, applies the compiled swiglu
activation, then un-sorts (`_scatter_unsort`). It is the `experts` slot's code path.

## Checklist

### A. `SwitchGLU.__call__` (`switch_layers.py:176-199`)

- **Callers:** `MoE.__call__` (`mobilemoe.py:230`, `y = self.experts(x, inds)`).
  Decode shapes (plain MLX): `x` [rows,1,768] bf16, `inds` [rows,1,4] uint32
  (`territory-model.md` §A from `bench/micro/breakdown.py:442-460`; slot flattens to
  [rows,768] / [rows,4] per `bench/grader/slots.py:107-114`). At 1/8/32 rows: x
  [1,1,768] / [8,1,768] / [32,1,768], inds [1,1,4] / [8,1,4] / [32,1,4].
- **Callees:** `mx.expand_dims` + `squeeze` (views, free); `_gather_sort` (B) and
  `_scatter_unsort` (C) only when `indices.size >= 64` (`:181`), i.e. rows×4 ≥ 64,
  i.e. 16+ rows; three `gather_qmm` calls via `TransposedQuantizedSwitchLinear`
  (`mobilemoe.py:172-184`, transpose=False, rhs_indices only) — one GatherQMM +
  one default-Arange kernel each; compiled `swiglu` (`activations.py:9-11`, one
  fused kernel). Kernel inventory matches exactly:
  `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md:136-139` — 7/layer at 1–8 rows
  (3×(Arange+GatherQMM) + silu-mul), 13/layer at 32 rows (+ Gather 60, ArgSort 40,
  FloorDivide 20 per step). The 867→987 op jump at 32 rows is all here
  (`tables.md:152-154`: +60 Gather, +40 ArgSort, +20 FloorDivide).
- **Data:** gate_w/up_w [60,768,48] uint32, scales/biases [60,768,12] bf16;
  down_w [60,384,96] uint32, scales/biases [60,384,24] bf16 (brief §experts).
  Sorted path: x [32,1,768] → [128,1,768] bf16, idx [128] uint32; gate/up out
  [128,1,384] bf16; down out [128,1,768] → unsorted to y [32,1,4,768] bf16.
  One expert = 0.553 MB (`bottleneck-explained.md` §4 worked example).
- **Neighbours:** before: router/top-4/weights (model territory) produce `inds`;
  after: combine weighting (`mobilemoe.py:231`) consumes `y` in `inds` order, plus
  the shared expert add. A replacement must keep y's (row, expert-slot) positions
  and the brief §experts rounding points (see Invariants).
- **Cost:** routed-experts knock-out: 0.92 ms @1 row, 14.67 ms @32 rows plain MLX
  (`step-breakdown.md:170,211`); 140 kernels/step @1 (6.6 µs each), 260 @32.
  Reads 51 MB @1 (must-read 44), 908 MB @32 (must-read 443, per-pair 1416)
  (`2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md:26,32`).
- **Invariants:** G2 experts: every element within 2 bf16 ulp of reference (floor at
  0.001); each product accumulates fp32 and rounds to bf16; `silu(gate)*up` is
  computed on bf16 values and rounded to bf16 before the down product (brief §experts);
  unsort must restore exact (row, slot) positions.

### B. `_gather_sort` (`switch_layers.py:12-17`)

- **Callers:** `SwitchGLU.__call__` (`:185`) when rows ≥ 16.
- **Callees:** `mx.argsort(indices)` → ArgSort (order); `mx.argsort(order)` →
  ArgSort (inv_order, a second full sort just to invert the permutation);
  `order // M` → FloorDivide; `x.flatten(0,-3)[order // M]` → Gather;
  `indices[order]` → Gather. Per layer at 32 rows: 2 ArgSort + 1 FloorDivide +
  2 Gather (`tables.md:136` ÷ 20 layers).
- **Data:** over 128 pairs: order/inv_order/idx [128] (uint32/int32), x gathered to
  [128,1,768] bf16 (196 KB/layer). rhs passed to `gather_qmm` ascending;
  `sorted_indices=True` sets MLX `right_sorted_` (`ops.cpp:5824-5825`, v0.32.4).
- **Neighbours:** before: expand_dims; after: the three products read sorted x/idx.
  On the critical chain (products wait for it).
- **Cost:** 5 kernels/layer on-chain (inv_order's argsort overlaps the products);
  no isolated knock-out — inside the 14.67 ms. CPU record for the whole experts
  glue rises 128 → 399 µs/step from 1 to 32 rows (`tables.md:99`).
- **Invariants:** sorted rhs must stay a permutation of the pairs (same multiset of
  (row, expert) pairs); stability across equal experts is irrelevant since pairs
  are distinguishable by row.

### C. `_scatter_unsort` (`switch_layers.py:20-24`)

- **Callers:** `SwitchGLU.__call__` (`:197`) when rows ≥ 16.
- **Callees:** `x[inv_order]` → Gather (1/layer, the third Gather in `tables.md:136`);
  `mx.unflatten` is a view (free).
- **Data:** [128,1,768] bf16 → [32,1,4,768] bf16 (196 KB/layer moved).
- **Neighbours:** before: down product; after: squeeze (view) → combine. On-chain.
- **Cost:** 1 kernel/layer, 20/step; ~6.81 µs each (`moe_parts` fixed-cost unit,
  `territory-runs.md` §`step_parts.txt`).
- **Invariants:** must restore exact pre-sort positions (combine pairs y with weights
  by slot).

### D. `QuantizedSwitchLinear.__call__` (`switch_layers.py:75-90`)

- **Callers:** nothing in the served int4 model — MobileMoE replaces all three
  projections with `TransposedQuantizedSwitchLinear` (`mobilemoe.py:200-214`).
  Same op, `transpose=True`, [E,out,in] layout; the live twin is
  `mobilemoe.py:172-184` (model territory §F).
- **Callees:** one `mx.gather_qmm(..., transpose=True, rhs_indices only,
  sorted_indices)` → GatherQMM + default lhs `arange` (`ops.cpp` `indices_or_default`,
  `tables.md:137-139` pattern). The bias add (`:88-89`) is absent in the served
  model (bias=False, `switch_layers.py:171-173`).
- **Data/Neighbours/Cost/Invariants:** as the live twin (see A/F of territory-model):
  fp32 accumulate, bf16 out; per-pair reads in MLX's qvm/qmv vector kernel below
  60 rows (see G).
- **Note:** kept for the unquantized→quantized conversion path (`to_quantized`,
  `:131-149`); not decode-time.

### E. `SwitchLinear` (`switch_layers.py:93-149`, unquantized)

- Not on the int4 decode path (`mx.gather_mm`, dense). Only its `to_quantized`
  constructor matters at conversion time. No checklist beyond this line.

### F. `SwitchMLP` (`switch_layers.py:202-236`)

- GELU variant; MobileMoE uses `SwitchGLU`. Same sort threshold (`:222`) and
  glue structure, but dead code for this model. No checklist beyond this line.

### G. MLX dispatch under `gather_qmm` (v0.32.4 source, read to fix the callees)

- `GatherQMM::eval_gpu` (`quantized.cpp:1980-2094`): the grouped path
  `gather_qmm_rhs` needs `M == 1 && B >= 16 && right_sorted_ && B/E >= 4`
  (`:2012`); else `M >= vector_limit` (4 when transpose=False, `:2005`) takes the
  matrix path; else the per-pair vector kernel (`gather_qvm`, `:2076-2093`).
- The port's call gives M=1, B=4·rows pairs, E=60, right_sorted_=True (sorted flag
  set, lhs not passed: `ops.cpp:5824-5825` + `primitives.h:1703-1710` wiring).
  `B/E >= 4` needs 240+ pairs = 60+ rows — never in decode (max 32). So **every**
  decode row count runs `gather_qvm`, whose grid is (M, N/64, B) threadgroups of
  64 threads (`quantized.cpp:1462-1500`): each pair's tiles read their expert's
  weights independently → per-pair reads. The sort changes locality, not kernel choice.
- The micro kernel-A/B experiment (`bench/micro/moe_parts.py:152-180`) slices
  weights to E experts, so B/E ≥ 4 there and sorted=True *does* switch kernels —
  its sorted/unsorted gaps measure the grouped kernel, not serving's sort. Noted
  on `ineff-runs-3`.

- **Feeds:** model territory — y [rows,1,4,768] bf16 in inds order to combine
  (`mobilemoe.py:231`).
- **Callees in:** quantized-kernels territory — GatherQMM/ArgSort/Gather/FloorDivide

{"content":"# Inefficiency: sort glue costs 6 kernels/layer from 16 rows, for locality only

- **Owner:** explorer-switch-layers
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:30Z
- **Next:** verifier to confirm kernel inventory and the B/E>=4 gate

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

When `indices.size >= 64` (`switch_layers.py:181`), i.e. 16+ decode rows,
`SwitchGLU` sorts the 4·rows pairs by expert (`_gather_sort`, `:12-17`) and
un-sorts afterwards (`_scatter_unsort`, `:20-24`). Per layer that is 2 ArgSort
(`order`, and a second full sort for `inv_order`), 1 FloorDivide (`order // M`),
and 3 Gathers (sorted x, sorted idx, unsort) — 6 kernels/layer, 120/step
(`results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md:136`: Gather 60, ArgSort 40,
FloorDivide 20; the 867→987 op jump at 32 rows).

The sort cannot change MLX's kernel choice in decode: the grouped path needs
`B/E >= 4` (`quantized.cpp:2012`, v0.32.4), i.e. 240+ pairs at E=60 = 60+ rows,
so every decode row count runs the per-pair `gather_qvm` kernel regardless
(see `territory-switch-layers.md` §G). Its only function in serving is cache
locality within that kernel (sorted serving reads 908 MB vs the 1416 MB
per-pair model — caches serve a third).

## Cost

Per decode step (plain MLX, 128-token prompts):

- 1 row: no sort runs (4 pairs < 64) — 0 kernels, 0 ms.
- 8 rows: no sort runs (32 pairs < 64) — 0 kernels, 0 ms.
- 32 rows: 120 kernels/step, ~5 of the 6 per layer on the critical chain
  (`inv_order`'s argsort overlaps the products). 5 × 6.81 µs × 20 layers
  = 0.68 ms ≈ 0.7 ms (fixed-cost unit from
  `results/runs/2026-10-30-micro/step_parts.txt`). Index/activation traffic is
  ~8 MB/step ≈ 0.04 ms at peak — negligible. No isolated knock-out; contained
  in the experts 14.67 ms (`step-breakdown.md:211`). CPU record for the experts
  glue rises 128 → 399 µs/step from 1 to 32 rows (`tables.md:99`).

## Kind

Overhead-bound: ~0.7 ms of fixed kernel costs moving ~8 MB.

## Spans

`switch-layers`, `quantized-kernels` (kernel fixed costs), `runs` (inventory).

## Predicted saving

Standalone removal would *lose* time (unsorted pairs lose the locality that
keeps a third of repeat reads in cache — size unmeasured in serving). The
saving is realizable only inside a fused grouped `experts` kernel that needs
no sort: then the full ~0.7 ms at 32 rows plus the 8 MB traffic go, jointly
with `ineff-runs-1` and `ineff-switch-layers-2` (one fix; savings do not add):

- 1 row: 0.0 ms (no sort runs).
- 8 rows: 0.0 ms (no sort runs).
- 32 rows: ≈ 0.7 ms (100 on-chain kernels × 6.81 µs).

{"content":"# Inefficiency: gate/up/down products and activation unfused

- **Owner:** explorer-switch-layers
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:30Z
- **Next:** verifier to confirm against the kernel inventory and brief rounding points

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

Each layer launches three separate `mx.gather_qmm` kernels (up, gate, down;
`switch_layers.py:188-194` via `mobilemoe.py:172-184`) plus one compiled
silu-mul activation kernel (`activations.py:9-11`, `tables.md:136,141`): 4
on-chain kernels/layer, 80/step at every row count, plus 3 off-chain default
`Arange` kernels/layer (60/step, measured ~free — `step-breakdown.md:438-463`).
Between them the gate, up and silu-mul bf16 outputs are written to memory and
re-read: at 32 rows 3 × [128,1,384] bf16 = 0.29 MB/layer = 5.9 MB/step; at 1
row 3 × [4,1,384] = 9 KB/layer. One fused kernel could do all three products
and the activation in registers/shared memory.

## Cost

Per decode step (plain MLX, 128-token prompts):

- 1 row: experts knock-out 0.92 ms for 140 kernels = 6.6 µs each
  (`step-breakdown.md:170,182`). Fixed-cost share of the 4 fusable kernels:
  4 × 6.81 µs × 20 = 0.54 ms; intermediates 0.2 MB ≈ 0.00 ms.
- 8 rows: same structure as 1 row (no sort; 867 ops, `tables.md:153`). No
  knock-out at 8 rows; fixed-cost share again ≈ 0.54 ms (estimate, same kernels).
- 32 rows: experts knock-out 14.67 ms (`step-breakdown.md:211`). Fixed-cost
  share of the 4 ≈ 0.54 ms; intermediates 5.9 MB ≈ 0.03 ms at peak. The rest of
  the 14.67 ms is per-pair weight reads (`ineff-runs-1`) and small-kernel
  efficiency, not this entry.

## Kind

Overhead-bound: 80 on-chain kernels/step doing 4 launches where 1 suffices.

## Spans

`switch-layers`, `quantized-kernels`.

## Predicted saving

Fusing the 3 products + activation into one kernel (keeping per-pair reads —
grouping is `ineff-runs-1`'s prize; one combined fix, savings do not add):

- 1 row: 3 launches/layer saved ≈ 3 × 6.81 µs × 20 = 0.4 ms.
- 8 rows: ≈ 0.4 ms (same kernel structure; estimate).
- 32 rows: ≈ 0.4 ms fixed costs + 5.9 MB intermediate traffic (0.03 ms at
  peak); larger threadgroups should also lift efficiency — unquantified.

A fused kernel must keep the boundary: fp32 accumulation + bf16 rounding per
product, silu-mul on bf16 values rounded to bf16 before the down product
(brief §experts).

## Verdict

(verifier to write)

Key dispatch finding: the grouped `gather_qmm_rhs` path needs `B/E >= 4` (`quantized.cpp:2012`), i.e. 240+ pairs at E=60 = 60+ rows — so every decode row count (1–32) runs the per-pair `gather_qvm` kernel, and the sort changes locality, never kernel choice.

39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
69|
70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
93|
94|## Tools and limits
95|
96|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
97|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
98|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes; stop one that hangs.
99|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.

177|## How each attempt is judged
178|
179|The pass criteria are the same as in the API-stage brief and were fixed before this session, as written here.
180|
181|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows.
182|2. **G2, correct.** It is tested on inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows.
183|   - **`routing`:** each row selects the same 4 experts. The only exception is a row whose 4th and 5th biased scores in the reference are within 1e-6 of each other; such rows are counted and reported. The weights, matched by expert, are within 1e-4 relative.
184|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element is within 2 bfloat16 units in the last place of the reference value. For values smaller than 0.001 in magnitude, the unit at 0.001 applies, so summing in a different order near zero is not a failure.
185|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
186|3. **G3, faster.** The decode step's period is the median over 3 repeats in shuffled order, with 128-token prompts, at 1, 8 and 32 requests. It must be lower than both the original model's and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code. The gap must exceed the spread between repeats.
187|
188|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
189|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
190|- or the correctness results, with counts and the worst example per check;
191|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer`: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, and `beats_compiled`.
192|
193|The piece timing runs the slot on all 20 layers' captured inputs and waits for the GPU once at the end. It takes the median of 30 repeats, per layer. It is a guide; G3 decides.
194|
195|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and beats the compiled reference in the piece timing at all three row counts, or after 5 attempts. 1|# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.
6|
7|## Hardware limits
8|
9|**Peak bandwidth**:
10|The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
11|_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed
12|
13|**Peak compute**:
14|The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
15|_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)
16|
17|**Achieved bandwidth**:
18|The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
19|_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)
20|
21|**Arithmetic intensity**:
22|Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
23|_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio
24|
25|**Ridge point**:
26|The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.
27|
28|**Roofline**:
29|The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.
30|
31|## Bottlenecks and fixes
32|
33|**Bandwidth-bound**:
34|A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.
35|
36|**Compute-bound**:
37|A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.
38|
39|**Overhead-bound**:
40|A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
41|_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)
42|
43|**Bottleneck**:
44|The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
45|_Avoid_: issue, slowness
46|
47|**Kernel**:
48|One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
49|_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)
50|
51|**Occupancy**:
52|The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
53|_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)
54|
55|**Knock-out**:
56|A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
57|_Avoid_: ablation
58|
59|**Baseline**:
60|The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.
61|
62|**Fix**:
63|One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
64|_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak
65|
66|## Inference
67|
68|**Prefill**:
69|Processing a request's whole prompt in one pass before any token is generated.
70|
71|**Decode step**:
72|One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.
73|
74|**Decode rows**:
75|The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
76|_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency
77|
78|**Client concurrency**:
79|The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.
80|_Avoid_: batch size
81|
82|## Mixture of experts
83|
84|**Expert**:
85|One of the interchangeable feed-forward blocks in a layer; MobileMoE-S has 60 routed experts per layer.
86|
87|**Active experts**:
88|The experts the router picks for one token in one layer (4 for MobileMoE-S).
89|_Avoid_: selected experts, top-k experts
90|
91|**Distinct experts**:
92|The number of different experts used by all decode rows together in one layer during one decode step; it decides how much expert weight data the step must read.
93|_Avoid_: unique experts, expert coverage
94|
95|## Models
96|
97|**MobileMoE-S**:
98|Meta's smallest on-device mixture-of-experts model (about 1.3B parameters in total, about 272M used per token), studied here in its SFT (full-precision) and QAT (int4) variants.
99|
100|**Muse Spark**:
101|Meta's hosted model. In this project it chooses which pieces of the decode step to replace and writes their kernels, working in its own Muse Spark session; it is never the model under study.
102|
103|**Muse Code**:
104|Meta's own coding agent for the terminal, built on Muse Spark; the only program in which Muse Spark does its work in this project.
105|_Avoid_: Muse CLI, Meta Code
106|
107|**Muse Spark session**:
108|A Muse Code session in which Muse Spark writes every turn, the lead's and every helper's, kept apart from Claude's work by its own branch, folder and commit trailer.
109|_Avoid_: guardrail (for the session itself), Meta mode
110|
111|## Muse Spark's work
112|
113|**Slot**:
114|One replaceable piece of the mixture-of-experts block (routing, combine, or the routed experts), with fixed inputs and outputs, that Muse Spark may replace with its own kernels.
115|_Avoid_: target (that is a slot Muse Spark has chosen), module
116|
117|**Round**:
118|One Muse Spark session in which a swarm explores and then builds, followed by Claude's independent measurement of what it produced.
119|_Avoid_: iteration, cycle
120|
121|**Swarm**:
122|All the agents of one round, the lead and its helpers, working toward one goal through shared documents that each of them reads and adds to.
123|_Avoid_: team, crew
124|
125|**Lead agent**:
126|The one agent of a swarm that starts the helpers, keeps the shared documents current, settles clashes and commits; it neither explores nor grades.
127|_Avoid_: orchestrator, main agent
128|
129|**Helper agent**:
130|An agent the lead starts: an explorer, the verifier, a builder or a boundary agent. It reports back and never commits.
131|_Avoid_: worker, subagent (when the role matters, not the mechanism)
132|
133|**Reminder agent**:
134|One of Muse Code's own background agents, which watch the lead's progress and may nudge it, for example to check a claim before it says it is done; Muse Spark writes their turns too, but they take no part in the work.
135|_Avoid_: helper (that is one the lead starts)
136|
137|**Exploration phase**:
138|The first part of a round, in which explorers map the code and the measurements and find where the decode step loses time.
139|
140|**Implementation phase**:
141|The second part of a round, in which builders write and grade solutions to the confirmed inefficiencies.
142|_Avoid_: hypothesis phase
143|
144|**Territory**:
145|The part of the code or the measurements that one explorer covers: a module, a single important file, or a measurement document.
146|_Avoid_: area, lens
147|
148|**Analysis**:
149|The swarm's shared account of the code, written during exploration: the context, how the territories feed each other, and the ranked inefficiencies, each with its cost and sources.
150|_Avoid_: diagnosis, findings (those are Claude's)
151|
152|**Inefficiency**:
153|One cause of lost time in the decode step: where it is in the code, what it costs, and what removing it should save. It is confirmed or refuted against its sources before anyone builds on it.
154|_Avoid_: issue, bottleneck (that is the single largest cause)
155|
156|**Hypothesis**:
157|A proposed solution to one inefficiency: the slot it replaces, the boundary it keeps and the saving it predicts, tested by competing attempts.
158|_Avoid_: strategy, plan
159|
160|**Boundary**:
161|What a solution must keep identical so that the steps before and after its slot work exactly as before: the slot's inputs and outputs, their dtypes, and the rounding points.
162|_Avoid_: interface (unqualified), contract
163|
164|**Attempt**:
165|A solution a builder has graded and the lead has committed; attempts for a slot are numbered in order and have no limit.
166|_Avoid_: try, submission, draft

188|    def __init__(self, args: ModelArgs):
189|        super().__init__()
190|        dim = args.hidden_size
191|        hidden = args.intermediate_size
192|        num_experts = args.num_local_experts
193|        self.top_k = args.num_experts_per_tok

195|        self.routed_scaling_factor = args.routed_scaling_factor

198|        self.expert_bias = mx.zeros((num_experts,))
199|        self.experts = SwitchGLU(dim, hidden, num_experts)
200|        if args.transposed_experts:
201|            q = args.quantization
202|            for name, dims in (
203|                ("gate_proj", (dim, hidden)),
204|                ("up_proj", (dim, hidden)),
205|                ("down_proj", (hidden, dim)),
206|            ):
207|                proj = TransposedQuantizedSwitchLinear(
208|                    *dims,
209|                    num_experts,
210|                    q["group_size"],
211|                    q["bits"],
212|                    q.get("mode", "affine"),
213|                )
214|                setattr(self.experts, name, proj)

217|    def __call__(self, x: mx.array) -> mx.array:
218|        # The reference computes the router in float32.
219|        scores = mx.sigmoid(self.router(x.astype(mx.float32)))
220|
221|        # The bias changes which experts are selected, not their weights.
222|        k = self.top_k
223|        biased = scores + self.expert_bias
224|        inds = mx.argpartition(-biased, kth=k - 1, axis=-1)[..., :k]

229|

1|# Inefficiency: experts re-reads expert weights per (token, expert) pair
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-runs
4|- **Status:** open

7|- **Next:** verifier to confirm against the knock-out table
8|
9|## Slot
10|
11|`experts`
12|
13|## What happens
14|
15|Each (token, expert) pair's `gather_qmm` reads that expert's gate/up/down weights afresh, so popular experts are re-read once per pair instead of once per step. The knock-out table (`results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`, "Each piece" rows) shows knocking out experts saves 908 MB of reads per step at 32 rows while the model must read only 443 MB for the distinct experts (per-pair model: 1416 MB). At 1 row the two agree (51 vs 44 MB) because all 4 pairs use distinct experts. Mechanism belongs to the switch-layers / quantized-kernels territories; this entry is the measurement.
16|
17|## Cost
18|
19|At 1, 8 and 32 rows, per decode step (plain MLX, 128-token prompts):
20|
21|- 1 row: experts costs 0.92 ms (knock-out, unrecorded) and reads 51 MB vs 44 MB must-read — excess 7 MB.
22|- 8 rows: no knock-out row; the whole step reads 685 MB vs 393 MB must-read (whole-step table), so the step-wide excess is 292 MB, of which experts is the largest piece by the r1/r32 pattern.
23|- 32 rows: experts costs 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step and reads 908 MB vs 443 MB must-read — excess 465 MB. Micro corroboration (`results/runs/2026-10-30-micro/moe_parts.txt`): experts 16.60 ms per 20 layers at R=32 vs 2.64 ms at peak bandwidth for the same bytes.
24|
25|## Kind
26|
27|Bandwidth-bound: the excess is bytes re-read, ~2× the necessary expert traffic at 32 rows. (The remaining ~12 ms of the 14.67 is kernel overhead and the necessary traffic, owned by the kernel territories.)
28|
29|## Spans
30|
31|`runs`, `switch-layers`, `quantized-kernels`
32|
33|## Predicted saving
34|
35|Excess bytes removed ÷ peak bandwidth (200 GB/s), per decode step:
36|
37|- 1 row: 7 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = 0.04 ms ≈ 0.0 ms (nothing lost to re-read at 1 row).
38|- 8 rows: scaled estimate — pairs scale 32/128 of r32, excess ≈ 465 × 32/128 = 116 MB → 0.6 ms.
39|- 32 rows: 465 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = 2.3 ms.
40|
41|Arithmetic is a floor (values the excess at peak bandwidth); the measured experts time is 14.67 ms, so the rest must come from overhead removal, not this entry.
42|
43|## Verdict

7|## Slot

11|## What happens
12|
13|Each layer's weighting (`third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:231-232`) launches
14|5 kernels: AsType (bf16 y→fp32 for the multiply), Multiply, Sum, AsType (back to bf16),

16|AsType 40, Multiply 20, Sum 20, Add 20). The two casts and the separate add exist only
17|because each op is its own kernel; the bf16↔fp32 round-trips are fused away by compiling
18|the block (`claude/findings/step-breakdown.md:426`).

22|- Kernels × fixed cost: 100 × ~6.1 µs @1 row (0.61 ms ÷ 100, measured) ≈ 0.61 ms.
23|  @32 rows the knock-out (0.33 ms) is below 100 × 7 µs = 0.7 ms, so at 32 rows the chain
24|  partly overlaps other work — the knock-out, not the kernel count, caps the saving there.
25|- Bytes ÷ peak: activations only — per layer y [32,4,768] bf16 (196 KB) + shared [32,768]
26|  bf16 (49 KB) + out 49 KB ≈ 0.3 MB/layer, ~5.9 MB/step @32 rows → 0.03 ms at peak.

28|  0.61 ms @1 row (13% of step), 0.33 ms @32 rows (1% of step).
29|  @8 rows not measured (`step-breakdown.md:91`); kernel inventory identical to 1 row
30|  (`tables.md:153`), cost estimated ~0.45 ms by interpolation.
31|- CPU record: 75 µs @1, 135 µs @32 per step (`tables.md:103`).
32|
33|## Kind
34|
35|Overhead-bound: pure chain of tiny elementwise kernels moving ~6 MB @32 rows.

39|`model` (the chain) → slot `combine`. Neighbours: `switch-layers` (y producer),
40|shared expert (E in territory-model, computed outside slots, consumed by the Add).

44|One fused kernel per layer (20 × 7 µs ≈ 0.14 ms residual). Saving per decode step:
45|0.61 − 0.14 ≈ **470 µs @1 row**; ~0.45 − 0.14 ≈ **300 µs @8 rows** (estimate);
46|0.33 − 0.14 ≈ **190 µs @32 rows**. Together with ineff-model-1, routing+combine are
47|1.63 ms of the 4.75 ms step @1 row (34%).

**How the vLLM column was read.** vLLM's one-request runs were disturbed by paging ([Limits](#limits)), so its savings are given as the range between two estimates: the median of the repeats and the fastest repeat. "Noise" marks pieces where an estimate is zero or below, or where the two differ by more than 0.3 ms and by more than a third of the larger.

What it shows, for plain MLX:

- **Most pieces cost 4–7 µs per kernel.**
  - Attention: 1.21 ms for 220 kernels, 5.5 µs each.
  - Routing: 1.02 ms for 240, 4.3 µs each.
  - Routed experts: 0.92 ms for 140, 6.6 µs each.
  - Combine: 0.61 ms for 100, 6.1 µs each.

  That matches the fixed cost of about 7 µs per dependent kernel measured in [decode-bottlenecks finding 2](decode-bottlenecks.md#2-with-one-request-the-step-is-about-870-kernels-in-a-chain). There are exceptions:
  - The attention kernel (20 µs each) and the o projection (13 µs) cost more.
  - RoPE's 40 kernels cost only 0.07 ms in all, because the rotations of q and of k don't wait for each other.
- **The mixture-of-experts block's bookkeeping costs more than its arithmetic.**
  - Routing and combine are 340 kernels and 1.63 ms, a third of the step.
  - The four routed experts' products cost 0.92 ms; the shared expert's 0.51 ms.
  - Fusing the bookkeeping ([decode-bottlenecks fix 1](decode-bottlenecks.md#what-to-do-in-priority-order)) targets the largest piece.
- **The output layer runs near peak bandwidth where it sits.**

The share is the saving over the step with every wrapper idle (28.40 ms in plain MLX, 30.31 ms in vLLM). With 32 rows both engines' repeats agree within 2.5%.

What it shows:

- **The routed experts take half the step,** 14.7 ms in plain MLX and 14.9 ms in vLLM.
  - The step needs 40 distinct experts per layer, 443 MB, which would take 2.2 ms at peak bandwidth.
  - The per-pair kernel reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair instead ([decode-bottlenecks finding 5](decode-bottlenecks.md#5-with-many-requests-experts-are-read-once-per-token-expert-pair)).
- **Attention is next:** 5.6 ms in plain MLX and 7.5 ms in vLLM. Its kernel is 3.1 and 4.3 ms of that.
- **The routing bookkeeping stops mattering**, at 1.5–1.7 ms. Its kernels don't grow with the number of rows, while the experts' work does.
- **Savings don't add up across pieces.** Removing a large piece changes how the rest of the step overlaps. Each knock-out also replays the same outputs, which changes the tokens generated and so the experts that later steps use. Read each figure as that piece's cost where it runs, not as a share of a whole.
- **vLLM's output layer saves twice as much as plain MLX's (5.1 against 2.5 ms), and the kernel is not the reason.**
  - Timed on its own, the output layer takes 2.35 ms for 32 rows in either engine's layout, with identical results (`lm_head_shapes.py`). vllm-metal hands the model one packed sequence (1 × 32 rows), plain MLX 32 sequences of 1.
  - The rest of vLLM's 5.1 ms comes from knocking it out inside vLLM's step, not from the layer itself. It is not explained here.
  - vLLM's top-level savings also add up to 33.3 ms, more than its 30.3 ms step; plain MLX's add up to 25.5 ms, less than its step, as overlapping pieces should. So at least one of vLLM's 32-row knock-outs removes more than its own piece's work.

**Derived from the measurements above**: the bytes the model must read, over measured times. The [next subsection](#memory-traffic-counted-by-the-gpu) checks them against the traffic the GPU counted. For each piece:

- **MB to read:** the weights it uses in one step, summed over the 20 layers. Only the experts the step's tokens picked count, each once. The attention kernel also reads the key/value cache up to each row's position (bfloat16, 1 KB per token per layer).
- **GFLOP:** its multiply-adds, counted as 2 operations each.
- **Achieved:** those bytes and operations over what the step saves without the piece, so the rate at which the piece does its work where it runs. Peaks are 200 GB/s and 5.2 TFLOP/s.

Activations are not counted, and a piece that reads the same weights twice is counted once, so the bandwidths are lower bounds on the real traffic. vLLM at one request is left out: its step is set by the CPU, so its savings are CPU time.

{"content":"# Territory: quantized-kernels

- **Owner:** explorer-quantized-kernels
- **Status:** exploring
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:40Z
- **Next:** post inefficiency entries, then mark done

## What it does

This territory is the `affine_gather_*` Metal kernels behind `mx.gather_qmm`
(`quantized.h`, `quantized_utils.h`). In MobileMoE-S decode they run the routed
experts' gate/up/down products: one `gather_qmm` each per layer per step, always
dispatched to `affine_gather_qvm` (proof below). 60 `GatherQMM` launches per step
at every row count (`results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md:152-154`).

## The checklist

### A. `affine_gather_qvm` + `qvm_impl` — the kernel decode actually runs

- **Callers:** `GatherQMM::eval_gpu` in
  `github.com/ml-explore/mlx`, tag `v0.32.4`,
  `mlx/backend/metal/quantized.cpp:1980-2094`. MobileMoE calls
  `mx.gather_qmm(..., transpose=False, group_size=32, bits=4, mode="affine")`
  with `x` `[pairs,1,K]` so `M=1` (`third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:172-184`,
  `switch_layers.py:176-199`). Dispatch: `M==1 < vector_limit==4`
  (`quantized.cpp:2005,2034`) rules out `gather_qmm`; the rhs fast path needs
  `M==1 && B>=16 && right_sorted_ && B/E>=4` (`quantized.cpp:2012`) but
  `B/E = rows*4/60 <= 2.1` at `rows<=32` (needs `rows>=60`), so it never fires;
  `transpose_==false` selects `gather_qvm` (`quantized.cpp:2073-2093`).
  Shapes at 1/8/32 rows: gate/up `M=1,N=384,K=768,B=rows*4`; down
  `M=1,N=768,K=384,B=rows*4`.
- **Callees:** `gather_qvm` launches `affine_gather_qvm` (`quantized.h:2355-2416`,
  via `quantized.cpp:1461-1529`) with `group_dims=(32,2,1)=64` threads,
  `bn = min(group_size,32)*2 = 64`, grid `(M,(N+63)/64,B)`: gate/up
  `(1,6,B)`, down `(1,12,B)`. Each threadgroup runs `qvm_impl`
  (`quantized.h:1222-1330`): 2 simdgroups x 32 lanes; each lane owns one K
  element per iteration and decodes 32 outputs via `qouter`
  (`quantized.h:452-553`, bits=4 path `:503-509`).
- **Data:** `w` uint32 `[E,in,out/8]` (4-bit, 8 per word along out),
  `scales`/`biases` bfloat16 `[E,in,out/32]`, `x` bfloat16 `[B,1,K]`,
  `rhs_indices` uint32 `[B]`, `y` bfloat16 `[B,1,N]`; per-pair offsets via
  `adjust_matrix_offsets` (`quantized.h:1636-1688`). Weights/scales read
  exactly once per pair: gate pair traffic = 6 tiles x 64 lanes x 24 iters x
  16 B weights = 144 KB = `768*384/2` B, scales+biases 36 KB; `x` row re-read
  12x per pair per product (each of 6 tiles' 2 simdgroups streams the full row:
  `qvm_impl:1275-1287`), ~55 KB x per pair over gate+up+down vs 3.75 KB needed.
- **Neighbours:** before: router `inds` (model territory) + `_gather_sort` at
  `indices.size>=64` (switch-layers; sort buys only L2 locality since rhs never
  fires). Between gate/up and down: activation (other-kernels). After: combine
  (model). Replacement must keep G2: every element within 2 bfloat16 ulp of the
  reference (1e-3 floor), float32 accumulation, bfloat16 rounding points.
- **Cost:** 60 launches/step (~6 us each: routed experts 140 kernels/0.92 ms @1,
  `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md:179-185`). Bytes (GPU counters,
  `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md:17-18`): experts saves
  51 MB read in 0.92 ms @1 (55 GB/s), 908 MB in 14.67 ms @32 (62 GB/s, 31% of
  peak). Grids @1 row are 24/24/48 threadgroups (~1.5-3K threads, ~5-10% of
  slots; whole-step Compute Occupancy 9%, same table).
- **Invariants:** `w = scale*q + bias` per group of 32 along out; output column
  `o` in word `o/8` bits `4*(o%8)` (brief); float32 accumulate, bfloat16 store
  (`qvm_impl:1324-1329`); fully K/N-aligned launches (384/768 % 64 == 0,
  768/384 % 32 == 0), no tail waste.

### B. `affine_gather_qmm_n` / `affine_gather_qmm_t` + `qmm_n_impl` / `qmm_t_impl` — never run in decode

- **Callers:** only `GatherQMM::eval_gpu` when `M >= vector_limit`
  (`quantized.cpp:2034-2051`); decode has `M=1`. Documented so no one chases them.
- **Callees:** `affine_gather_qmm_n` (`quantized.h:2501-2568`) /
  `_t` (`:2418-2499`), `BM=BN=BK=32`, `QuantizedBlockLoader`
  (`quantized.h:665-791`) + `BlockMMA`, `gemm_loop_*` (`quantized_utils.h:6-90`).
- **Data / Neighbours / Cost / Invariants:** same dtypes and `scale*q+bias`
  decoding as (A); zero cost in decode.

### C. `affine_gather_qmm_rhs` + `schedule_row_tile` — never run in decode

- **Callers:** only when `M==1 && B>=16 && right_sorted_ && B/E>=4`
  (`quantized.cpp:2012-2032`); needs `rows>=60`, unreachable at `rows<=32`.
  This is the kernel that would batch same-expert pairs (offsets +
  `schedule_row_tile`, `utils.h:501-542`); its absence is why each pair keeps
  its own grid (see ineff-quantized-kernels-1).
- **Callees:** `affine_gather_qmm_rhs` (`quantized.h:2570-2718`), `BM=16,BN=32,
  BK=32`, same loader/MMA helpers as (B).
- **Data / Neighbours / Cost / Invariants:** same as (A); zero cost in decode.
  Note for switch-layers: model sorts at `>=16` rows but dispatch ignores
  sortedness below `B/E>=4`.

### D. `affine_gather_qmv_fast` / `affine_gather_qmv` — never run in decode

- **Callers:** only when `transpose_==true` and `M < vector_limit`
  (`quantized.cpp:2053-2071`); MobileMoE uses `transpose=False`.
- **Callees:** `qmv_fast_impl` (`quantized.h:850-962`) / `qmv_impl` (`:964-1123`)
  via `affine_gather_qmv_fast` (`:2231-2291`) / `affine_gather_qmv` (`:2293-2353`).
- **Data / Neighbours / Cost / Invariants:** non-transposed `[E,out,in]` layout
  only; zero cost in decode.

### E. Shared helpers

- `dequantize` (`quantized.h:557-663`), `qdot`/`qdot_safe` (`:221-450`),
  `load_vector`/`load_vector_safe` (`:28-219`): per-bit paths, bits=4 used.
- `QuantizedBlockLoader` (`:665-791`): dequantize-on-load into threadgroup
  memory; used by (B)/(C), not by (A).
- `adjust_matrix_offsets` gather variant (`:1636-1688`): per-threadgroup index
  lookup, negligible cost.
- `gemm_loop_aligned/unaligned/finalize` (`quantized_utils.h:6-90`): the
  K-loop for (B)/(C) only.

## Relations

- Feeds from: model (router `inds`, `x`), switch-layers (`_gather_sort` order).
- Feeds to: other-kernels (activation reads gate/up outputs), model (combine
  reads `y`).
- Shared expert uses non-gather quantized matmul: other-kernels territory.

## Inefficiencies

- `ineff-quantized-kernels-1`: per-pair qvm grids run expert traffic at ~1/3 peak.
- `ineff-quantized-kernels-2`: three launches per pair + intermediate round-trips.

- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md`,

- `muse-spark/exploration/ineff-runs-1.md`, `ineff-runs-3.md`,

{"content":"# Inefficiency: each (token, expert) pair runs its own qvm grid at ~1/3 peak bandwidth

- **Owner:** explorer-quantized-kernels
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:45Z
- **Next:** verifier to confirm dispatch lines and the GB/s arithmetic

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

Every routed-expert product in decode runs `affine_gather_qvm`
(`quantized.h:2355-2416` + `qvm_impl`, `:1222-1330`): `M=1` rules out the matrix
path and `B/E<=2.1 < 4` rules out the rhs batched path forever at `rows<=32`
(`quantized.cpp:2005-2093 @v0.32.4`; full proof in
`territory-quantized-kernels.md` section A). Consequences, all in this kernel:

1. Each pair re-reads its expert's full weights through its own grid (gate/up 6
   threadgroups, down 12, 64 threads each). At 32 rows, 128 grids per product
   stream 908 MB for 443 MB of distinct experts.
2. Lanes read strided: consecutive lanes sit `out_vec_size_w` apart (gate: 192 B
   stride for 16 B loads, `qvm_impl:1262`), scales `out_vec_size_g` apart (12
   elements, 2 B used per 24 B stride, `:1263-1264`) — poor DRAM coalescing.
3. Each pair's `x` row is re-read 12x per product (every tile's 2 simdgroups
   stream the full K row, `:1275-1287`): ~55 KB x per pair vs 3.75 KB needed,
   ~131 MB/step excess at 32 rows, inside the 908 MB.
4. At 1 row the grids are 24/24/48 threadgroups (~1.5-3K threads, ~5-10% of the
   16-core GPU's slots): occupancy-starved.

## Cost

Per decode step, plain MLX (GPU counters
`results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md:17-18`, knock-outs
`results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md:210-213,259-262`):

- 1 row: 60 GatherQMM launches x ~6 us (`step-breakdown.md:179-185`: routed
  experts 140 kernels / 0.92 ms) ~ 0.36 ms; 51 MB read in 0.92 ms = 55 GB/s.
- 8 rows: no serving knock-out; bytes modelled 383 MB/pair-traffic
  (540 KB weights + 55 KB x per pair x 32 pairs x 20 layers); micro chained
  products 5.08 ms per 20 layers unsorted (`moe_parts.txt:6`) = ~75 GB/s.
- 32 rows: 908 MB read in 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step = 62 GB/s, 31% of peak.

## Kind

Overhead-bound at 1 row (51 MB needs 0.26 ms at peak; measured 0.92 ms; tiny
grids); bandwidth-bound at low efficiency at 8/32 rows (streaming kernel at
~1/3 peak: arithmetic intensity ~3 FLOP/B << ridge point 26, `GLOSSARY.md`).

## Spans

`quantized-kernels` (kernel + dispatch) -> slot `experts`. Measurements shared
with `runs`; sort interaction with `switch-layers`.

## Predicted saving

A fused kernel batching same-expert pairs with coalesced reads (the design
`gather_qmm_rhs` was built for but never fires) runs the same traffic at a
normal streaming rate, ~150 GB/s (the output layer hits 158 GB/s where it sits,
`step-breakdown.md:193-195`). Same bytes at 150 GB/s, per decode step:

- 1 row: 51 MB: 0.92 - 0.34 = 0.58, minus ~0.1 ms residual (4 pairs stay small)
  = **0.5 ms**.
- 8 rows: 383 MB: 5.08 - 2.55 = **2.5 ms** (micro baseline, caveat below).
- 32 rows: 908 MB: 14.67 - 6.05 = **8.6 ms**.

Overlap: complementary to `ineff-runs-1` (removes 465 MB of the 908 for 2.3 ms
at peak; combined ideal 443 MB @150 ~ 3.0 ms, total prize ~11.5 ms, consistent).
At 8 rows overlaps `ineff-runs-3` (its 1.3 ms sorting prize is part of this
2.5 ms via locality; net-new ~1.2 ms). Launch overhead shared with
`ineff-quantized-kernels-2` (~0.2 ms, count once).
Caveat at 8 rows: micro used 8 experts and chained calls, not serving's
distinct count and glue; serving prize may differ (same caveat as `ineff-runs-3`).

## Verdict

(verifier to write)

{"content":"# Inefficiency: gate/up/down are three qvm launches per pair with DRAM round-trips between

- **Owner:** explorer-quantized-kernels
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:45Z
- **Next:** verifier to confirm launch counts and intermediate sizes

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

Each layer launches 3 `GatherQMM` kernels (gate, up, down: 60/step at every row
count, `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md:152-154`) because each
product is its own `affine_gather_qvm` grid (`quantized.h:2355-2416`). Gate/up
outputs (`[B,1,384]` bfloat16 each) are written to DRAM, re-read by the
activation kernel, whose output is written and re-read by down: ~3.8 KB
intermediate traffic per pair per layer (weights-independent). A fused kernel
keeps all of it on-chip and launches once (gate+up share `x` and `rhs_indices`).

## Cost

Per decode step, plain MLX:

- Launches x fixed cost: 60 GatherQMM x ~6 us (`step-breakdown.md:179-185`)
  ~ 0.36 ms at 1, 8 and 32 rows; fusion to 1 launch/layer saves 40 x 6 us
  ~ 0.24 ms.
- Intermediate bytes: 3.8 KB x pairs x 20 layers = 0.3 / 2.4 / 9.8 MB at
  1/8/32 rows (counter corroboration: experts saves 26 MB written at 32 rows,
  `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md:18`).
- Measured experts totals: 0.92 ms @1, ~5.1 ms @8 (micro, `moe_parts.txt:6`),
  14.67 ms @32.

## Kind

Overhead-bound: launch count plus small round-trips (~10 MB at 32 rows vs 908 MB
the piece reads).

## Spans

`quantized-kernels` -> slot `experts`. Neighbour `other-kernels` (activation
kernel between the launches).

## Predicted saving

40 fewer launches (~0.24 ms) + intermediates on-chip (~10 MB @150 GB/s ~ 0.07 ms
@32), per decode step: **0.2 ms @1 row, 0.3 ms @8 rows, 0.3 ms @32 rows**.
Overlap: the launch saving is shared with `ineff-quantized-kernels-1`'s fused
ideal (its 150 GB/s assumes fusion); count the ~0.2 ms once. No overlap with
`ineff-runs-1`/`ineff-runs-3` (weight bytes, not launches).

## Verdict

(verifier to write)

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write a faster MobileMoE-S decode kernel
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
12|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
13|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
14|
15|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
16|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
17|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
18|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
19|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
20|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
21|
22|## The slots
23|
24|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the step: 1 to 32 in decode. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
25|
26|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
27|
28|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
29|
30|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
31||---|---|---|---|
32|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
33|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
34|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
35|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
36|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
37|
38|Reference:
39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
69|
70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
93|

1|# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.
6|
7|## Hardware limits
8|
9|**Peak bandwidth**:
10|The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
11|_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed
12|
13|**Peak compute**:
14|The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
15|_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)
16|
17|**Achieved bandwidth**:
18|The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
19|_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)
20|
21|**Arithmetic intensity**:
22|Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
23|_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio
24|
25|**Ridge point**:
26|The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.
27|
28|**Roofline**:
29|The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.
30|
31|## Bottlenecks and fixes
32|
33|**Bandwidth-bound**:
34|A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.
35|
36|**Compute-bound**:
37|A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.
38|
39|**Overhead-bound**:
40|A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
41|_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)
42|
43|**Bottleneck**:
44|The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
45|_Avoid_: issue, slowness
46|
47|**Kernel**:
48|One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
49|_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)
50|
51|**Occupancy**:
52|The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
53|_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)
54|
55|**Knock-out**:
56|A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
57|_Avoid_: ablation
58|
59|**Baseline**:
60|The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.
61|
62|**Fix**:
63|One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
64|_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak
65|
66|## Inference
67|
68|**Prefill**:
69|Processing a request's whole prompt in one pass before any token is generated.
70|
71|**Decode step**:
72|One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.
73|
74|**Decode rows**:
75|The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
76|_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency
77|
78|**Client concurrency**:
79|The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.
80|_Avoid_: batch size
81|
82|## Mixture of experts
83|
84|**Expert**:
85|One of the interchangeable feed-forward blocks in a layer; MobileMoE-S has 60 routed experts per layer.
86|
87|**Active experts**:
88|The experts the router picks for one token in one layer (4 for MobileMoE-S).
89|_Avoid_: selected experts, top-k experts
90|
91|**Distinct experts**:
92|The number of different experts used by all decode rows together in one layer during one decode step; it decides how much expert weight data the step must read.
93|_Avoid_: unique experts, expert coverage
94|
95|## Models
96|
97|**MobileMoE-S**:

1|# Inside a decode step, piece by piece
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|[Where a decode step's time goes](decode-bottlenecks.md) found that a decode step is hundreds of small GPU kernels, and that vLLM adds little over plain MLX. It timed parts of the step on their own. This document measures every piece inside the real step, in vLLM and in plain MLX side by side:
6|
7|- **inside vllm-metal's model runner:** the scheduler, building the batch, calling the model, encoding the GPU work, sampling and waiting;
8|- **inside the model:** each projection, norm, RoPE, cache write and attention kernel, the router, the routed experts, the combine, the shared expert and the output layer.
9|
10|For each piece it reports the GPU kernels it launches, the CPU time it takes to build, and what the step saves without it. It then lists the work that is repeated in every step for nothing, and measures what removing it saves.
11|
12|[bottleneck-explained.md](bottleneck-explained.md) explains these results in plain English, with the expert, attention and split-K byte counts worked through step by step.
13|
14|Everything was measured on 2026-11-01, and the GPU counters on 2026-11-02, on the baseline's machine, software and int4 model ([method](../benchmark/method.md)). Each claim is marked **measured** (timed here), **from the code** (read in the source) or **estimate** (reasoned from those two). The scripts are in [bench/micro/](../../bench/micro/): `breakdown.py`, `breakdown_tables.py`, `repeat_fixes.py`, `lm_head_shapes.py` and `gpu_counters.py`. The raw data is in [results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/](../../results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/) and [results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/](../../results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/), and every number below is in their `tables.md` files ([breakdown](../../results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md), [counters](../../results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md)).
15|
16|## Summary
17|
18|- **The scheduler and the rest of vLLM's runner are small.**
19|  - vLLM's scheduler takes 0.06 ms per step with one request and 0.30 ms with 32.
20|  - Everything the runner does outside the model takes 0.5 ms with one request and 1.6 ms with 32.
21|  - The CPU time goes to the model: recording its graph (2.4–3.1 ms) and encoding it into GPU commands (4.1–6.5 ms).
22|- **vLLM's step is 7–20% longer than plain MLX's, and the difference is in attention.**
23|  - On the same harness and model, vLLM is 19% slower with one request, 7–8% slower with 8 and 32, and 20% (6.5 ms) slower with 1,024-token prompts at 32 requests. The earlier "5–10%" compared different harnesses, on short prompts only.
24|  - vllm-metal's attention path runs about 1 ms of Python per step outside the kernels, against 0.23 ms in plain MLX.
25|  - It adds 60 copies of q, k and v per step, and 120 from 2 rows up.
26|  - Its attention kernel falls further behind as the context grows.
27|- **With one request, plain MLX's step is its chain of kernels.**
28|  - Most pieces cost 4–7 µs per kernel where they run.
29|  - The mixture-of-experts block's bookkeeping, routing and combine, costs 1.6 ms. That is more than its expert products, at 0.9 ms.
30|  - The output layer reads its 61.6 MB at about 158 GB/s, close to peak.
31|- **With 32 requests, the routed experts take half the step:** 14.7 of 28.4 ms in plain MLX and 14.9 of 30.3 ms in vLLM. Attention comes next, at 5.6 and 7.5 ms.
32|- **The GPU is busy 92–98% of the time but moves only 17–28% of its peak memory bandwidth** (measured with the GPU's own counters).
33|  - With one request each weight is read once: 193 MB per step against the 180 MB the model needs. Only the output layer comes close to peak, at about 160 GB/s. The other pieces' kernels read too little each to get past their fixed cost.
34|  - From 8 requests up, the step reads 1.7–2.2 times what the model needs. At 32 requests the routed experts read 908 MB from memory against the 443 MB they need: about half their repeat reads per (token, expert) pair reach memory, the rest come from cache.
35|  - At 32 requests MLX's split quantized products also write about 170 MB of partial sums per step.
36|  - While busy, the GPU's arithmetic units are 14–45% used and most of its thread slots are empty.
37|- **The repeated work is real but cheap.**
38|  - Three changes that leave the outputs bit-identical remove 140 of vLLM's 967 kernel operations per step.
39|  - They save 0.17 ms per step at 8 requests (1.2%). Where a gain stood clear of the run-to-run noise, it was at most 1.5% of the step.
40|  - Kernels that wait on nothing (an index range, a cast of a stored parameter) run alongside the chain, so removing them saves little.

44|`bench/micro/breakdown.py` runs the int4 model in two engines, each in its own process:

51|- 1,024-token prompts at 32 rows;

63|      target_forward  the model records its graph      target_forward

95|- **Span:** one named piece of the step, timed from entry to exit. Its **self time** leaves out the spans inside it.
96|- **Recording the graph:** the model's Python code records MLX operations. No GPU work happens yet.
97|- **Encoding:** `mx.async_eval` turns the recorded operations into GPU commands on the CPU, and hands them to the GPU.

381|## 4. Where vLLM differs from plain MLX
382|
383|**Kernels (measured, one counted step).** vLLM's step has 968 kernel operations with one request, against plain MLX's 867, and 1,088 against 987 with 32. The whole difference is in attention:
384|
385|| Operation | Per step | Where | Launches a kernel? |
386||---|---:|---|---|
387|| `Gather` | +60 | `queries[0]`, `keys[0]` and `values[0]` in vllm-metal's `sdpa_forward` (`attention/impls/sdpa.py:722-724`) | yes. In Python, `x[0]` becomes a gather, which copies, not a view (MLX `python/src/indexing.cpp:105-110,164`) |
388|| `Contiguous` | +60 | `mx.contiguous(...)` on the same lines | only from 2 rows up. With one row the transposed array is already laid out in order, so MLX shares its memory (`mlx/backend/gpu/primitives.cpp:50-62`, `mlx/backend/common/utils.h:204-206`) |
389|| `ReshapeAndCache` in place of 2 `SliceUpdate` | −20 | the cache write | yes |
390|| `PagedAttention` in place of `ScaledDotProductAttention` | 0 | the attention kernel | yes |
391|| `AsType` | +1 | the runner's inputs | yes |
392|
393|vLLM's graph also has 140–220 more view operations per step (706 against 566 with one row): squeezes, transposes and cache views. They launch no kernel but cost CPU to record and encode.
394|
395|**CPU (measured, cpu mode).** With one request, vLLM spends 2–3 ms more CPU per step than plain MLX:
396|
397|- **0.5 ms in the runner** ([section 2](#2-inside-vllm-metals-model-runner)).
398|- **0.7–1.0 ms more recording the model's graph.** Almost all of it is attention: vllm-metal's attention path takes 1,340 µs per step against plain MLX's 558:
399|  - `sdpa_forward` and the wrapper's own code: 564 µs, against 233 µs for plain MLX's whole attention code;
400|  - `prepare_sdpa_qkv`, around the projections and norms: 250 µs;
401|  - the RoPE helper, around the RoPE kernels: 161 µs;
402|  - the metadata lookup and the copies: 49 µs.
403|
404|  vLLM's cache write is cheaper: 31 µs against plain MLX's 134 µs.
405|- **1.1–1.5 ms more encoding**: 4.10 against 2.61 ms, and 3.68 ms in vLLM's least disturbed repeat.
406|  - vLLM's graph has 101 more kernel operations and 140 more views to encode.
407|  - vllm-metal's own two operations cost no more to encode than MLX's. Run piece by piece, its attention kernel took 0.62 ms per step to encode against 0.60 ms, and its cache write 0.58 against 0.76 ms.
408|  - Part of the gap may be paging, which counts as CPU time. Plain MLX's one-request runs saw no swapping; vLLM's always did.
409|
410|Plain MLX's step with one request has about 0.7 ms of CPU to spare. vLLM's extra CPU uses that up and then lengthens the step, which is why one request shows the largest relative gap.

412|**GPU (measured, knock-outs at 32 rows, where the GPU sets the pace).**
413|- vLLM's attention costs 7.5 ms per step in place, against plain MLX's 5.6 ms.
414|- Its kernel accounts for 4.3 ms against 3.1 ms, and the 60 copies in front of it for 0.24 ms.
415|- With 1,024-token prompts the step gap reaches 6.5 ms ([section 1](#1-vllm-against-plain-mlx-on-the-same-harness)). 452|So:
453|- **What clearly beats the spread:**
454|  - in plain MLX, 0.06–0.07 ms at 1 and 8 rows (1.3% and 0.5%);
455|  - in vLLM at 8 rows, 0.21 ms (1.5%) from the q, k and v views, and 0.17 ms with everything.

458|  - The row-index change leaves 32 rows untouched: the sorted path keeps MLX's default, with the same 986 operations. Yet it too came out 0.04 ms slower.
459|  - Each variant ran at a different time while the machine paged, so drift between variants can exceed the unchanged step's own spread. About 0.1 ms at 32 rows is the floor for any claim.

461|**Why so little (from the code, and an estimate).**
462|- **From the code:** MLX's Metal backend dispatches kernels concurrently. It puts a barrier only before a kernel that reads what an earlier kernel wrote (`mlx/backend/metal/device.cpp:371`, `:409-421`, `:606`).
463|- **Estimate:** an index range and the cast of a stored bias read nothing that the step computes. So they can run alongside the chain, and removing them saves little GPU time; what they cost is mainly encoding.
464|- The q, k and v copies are on the chain, since the attention kernel waits for them, which is why removing them shows.
465|
466|The kernel count is therefore a rough guide. What sets the step is the chain of kernels that wait for each other, plus the CPU time to record and encode all of them.

471|
472|- **Fix 1, compiling the mixture-of-experts block, stays first.** With one request, routing and combine are the largest piece, 1.6 ms of a 4.75 ms step. They are chains of tiny dependent kernels, which is what compiling fuses.

474|  - vLLM's one-request step is set by the CPU, and its attention path alone runs about 1 ms of Python per step.
475|  - Caching each layer's attributes, building the RoPE positions once per step, and `squeeze(0)` are all small Python changes in vllm-metal.
476|- **The three exact fixes in section 5 are worth making as clean-ups, not as speed-ups.**
477|  - They save 0.2 ms per step at most.
478|  - The q, k and v view change is the one with a measured gain, and it is a three-line change in vllm-metal.
479|  - Storing `expert_bias` in float32 belongs in `bench/convert_qat.py`. The row indices need an MLX change to help from 16 rows up.
480|- **Fixes 4 and 5 are confirmed where they run.**
481|  - The routed experts are half the step at 32 rows (14.7–14.9 ms).
482|  - The GPU's counters put fix 4's target at 465 MB per step of repeat expert reads that reach memory, 30% of the step's reads at 32 rows. That is smaller than the 973 MB of repeat reads, because the caches serve the rest.
483|  - vLLM's attention kernel costs 4.3 ms at 32 rows with 128-token prompts.
484|  - The engines' gap reaches 6.5 ms with 1,024-token prompts.
485|- **A new lead, not yet a fix: MLX's split quantized products.**
486|  - From 14 rows, the q, k, v and o projections and the shared expert write about 173 MB of float32 partial sums per step, which a second kernel adds up.
487|  - Measured for the q, k and v projections and the shared expert; worked out from the code for the o projection.
488|  - A smaller split, or partial sums in bfloat16, would cut that traffic, but would change how many threads run at once and, for bfloat16, the rounding. Neither has been tried.
489|- **None of this makes the step bandwidth-bound.** The GPU is busy 92–98% of the time at 17–28% of peak bandwidth, with most thread slots empty. Fewer, larger kernels (fixes 1 and 4) stay the main lever.
490|
491|## Limits
492|
493|- **Memory.** The machine paged heavily throughout.
494|  - Docker's VM was quit for the runs, but other programs held most of the 16 GB, among them a 2 GB `llama-server`.
495|  - Swap in use stayed between 24.7 and 31.1 GB.
496|  - During the runs the machine swapped out 8,622 pages a second (about 140 MB/s) on average while plain MLX ran, and 18,118 (about 300 MB/s) while vLLM ran.
497|  - vllm-metal's startup memory check refused the 1 GiB key/value cache twice, because forcing 512 MiB resident pushed other programs' memory out ([console log](../../results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/console-vllm-probe-refused.txt)). So vLLM ran with that check off (`VLLM_METAL_KV_COMMIT_PROBE=0`); the per-run swap counts recorded the paging instead.
498|- **vLLM's one-request runs are noisy.**
499|  - Its repeats spread by 17–47%, against 0.2–3.3% for plain MLX at every setting and 1.1–2.6% for vLLM at 8 and 32 rows.
500|  - In the worst repeats, single steps stalled for up to 124 ms.
