235|**Estimate: the possible saving.** A kernel that reads each key/value head once should cost about what 4/4 costs. That gives (569 − 247) µs × 20 = up to 6.4 ms less per step at 1,024-token prompts with 32 requests. This is an upper estimate, because 4/4 also does a third of the arithmetic.

237|**From the code.** Even with the layout added, the GQA kernel is only admitted when the batch has enough long partitions: full partitions × query heads ≥ 33 × GPU cores (`paged_attention.cpp:156`). The gain would show mainly at long contexts.

250|## How far this reaches
251|
252|**Who pays.** Every MobileMoE-S request served by vllm-metal pays these costs, and nothing reports it. The attention fallback is silent, and the compiled-MLP option only logs when it wraps something.
253|
254|**It is not specific to MobileMoE-S** (from the code, not measured):
255|
256|- MLX's rule applies to every mixture-of-experts model run through `gather_qmm`. With E experts, the grouped kernel needs 4E pairs.
257|- The GQA list also misses Meta's Llama 3.2 1B (32/8/64) and 3B (24/8/128).
258|- Compiled MLP covers two model families.

261|
262|| Problem | Owner |
263||---|---|
264|| Expert kernel choice | MLX |
265|| Attention head layouts | vllm-metal's Metal kernels |
266|| Mixture-of-experts block fusion | vllm-metal's compiled-MLP policy |
267|| Projection fusion | the port and `bench/convert_qat.py` |

269|**Health:**
270|
271|- **Maintainability: fragile.** A model gets the fast paths only if someone registers it in three places: a C++ table, Metal kernel instantiations and a Python class list. MLX's rule is an untuned `TODO`.
272|- **Correctness: healthy. Speed: at risk.** The fallbacks give correct results; the serving check found no failures in 80 requests. But they cost up to 2.3 times in attention and up to 36% in expert time, with no signal.

304|- Reaching the 0.9 ms bandwidth floor at one request would need whole layers fused into a few kernels, which is beyond this project's deadline.

306|## Using the Muse Spark credits
307|
308|> **Superseded on 2026-11-02.** Muse Spark now writes GPU kernels against these bottlenecks as a coding agent of its own, instead of only explaining them ([ADR 0004](../adr/0004-muse-spark-as-claude-code-agent.md)). The plan below is kept as it was written on 2026-10-30.
309|
310|Muse Spark (the Meta Model API) is used here only to explain, never as the model under study ([GLOSSARY.md](../GLOSSARY.md)). This analysis changes where to point it. The slow parts are not in vLLM's scheduler or runner, which take 0.5–1.6 ms per step ([step-breakdown.md](step-breakdown.md#2-inside-vllm-metals-model-runner)). They are in MLX's kernel choice, vllm-metal's per-model fast paths and the model's kernel count. Asking it about vLLM's scheduler would chase the wrong layer.
311|
312|**Plan for `analysis/explain.py`** (not written yet):
313|
314|1. **Inputs.** Send one focused packet per bottleneck above (sections 2, 4, 5 and 6). Each packet holds the measured numbers, the exact source excerpts cited here, and one question.
315|2. **Settings.** Use temperature 0 and a fixed answer format: claim, evidence lines, confidence, and the experiment that would confirm it.
316|   - Cache each answer by a hash of its packet.
317|   - Log token usage per call.
318|   - Read the key from `MODEL_API_KEY` in `.env`.
319|3. **Questions:**
320|   - an explanation for the report;
321|   - a design review: how to add 12/4/64 to the GQA kernel, what MLX's rule should be for 60 experts with 4 per token, and a sketch of a grouped decode expert kernel with `mx.fast.metal_kernel`;
322|   - an adversarial pass: "what else explains these numbers?", for example GPU clock behaviour.
323|4. **Output.** Save each answer in `analysis/findings/NN-*.md`, with a "verified by" line filled in only after a measurement confirms it. Model claims about kernel details are often wrong; the measurements decide.
324|
325|**Cost.** Meta's docs list a context window of about one million tokens ([Meta Model API docs](https://ai.developer.meta.com/docs/models/)). Press reports put the price at $1.25 per million input tokens and $4.25 per million output tokens ([AI Weekly](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/meta-prices-muse-spark-11-api-at-125425-per-m-tokens), [Modelcompare](https://modelcompare.dev/models/meta/muse-spark-1-1)); this was not checked on the official pricing page. At those prices, a call with 60k tokens in and 4k out costs about $0.09, so 20 calls cost under $2.

491|## Limits
492|
493|- **Memory.** The machine paged heavily throughout.
494|  - Docker's VM was quit for the runs, but other programs held most of the 16 GB, among them a 2 GB `llama-server`.
495|  - Swap in use stayed between 24.7 and 31.1 GB.
496|  - During the runs the machine swapped out 8,622 pages a second (about 140 MB/s) on average while plain MLX ran, and 18,118 (about 300 MB/s) while vLLM ran.
497|  - vllm-metal's startup memory check refused the 1 GiB key/value cache twice, because forcing 512 MiB resident pushed other programs' memory out ([console log](../../results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/console-vllm-probe-refused.txt)). So vLLM ran with that check off (`VLLM_METAL_KV_COMMIT_PROBE=0`); the per-run swap counts recorded the paging instead.
498|- **vLLM's one-request runs are noisy.**
499|  - Its repeats spread by 17–47%, against 0.2–3.3% for plain MLX at every setting and 1.1–2.6% for vLLM at 8 and 32 rows.
500|  - In the worst repeats, single steps stalled for up to 124 ms.
501|  - At one request vLLM's step is set by the CPU, so any CPU disturbance shows. Plain MLX had CPU to spare.
502|  - Hence the ranges and "noise" entries in section 3. `tables.md` also gives every knock-out from the fastest repeat.
503|- **The sync mode's times are not used.**
504|  - Run piece by piece, the GPU idles between pieces, and each piece starts cold.
505|  - The encoding and GPU times sum to 5–8 times the real step: plain MLX's GPU sum is 23.4 ms against a 4.72 ms step with one row. Only the kernel counts are used; the times are in `tables.md` for completeness.
506|- **Kernel counts are graph operations.** A `Contiguous` copy whose input is already laid out in order shares its memory and launches nothing; that is the case for vLLM's 60 at one row (from the code).
507|- **Knock-outs measure a piece where it runs.**
508|  - A faster version of the piece gains less than its full saving.
509|  - Removing a large piece changes the overlap of the rest, and the replayed outputs change the tokens generated. Savings at 32 rows are therefore not additive (section 3).
510|- **No per-kernel GPU trace.** The GPU side comes from step periods, knock-outs and whole-GPU counters, not from a timeline of each kernel. The GPU clock was not recorded, so whether the GPU ran at full clock is not known.
511|- **The GPU counters ([Memory traffic counted by the GPU](#memory-traffic-counted-by-the-gpu)):**
512|  - **Recording changes the step.** Recording only the counters cost plain MLX 3–9% of its step time at 1 and 32 requests in an interleaved check. Recorded vLLM steps were 1–6% longer than unrecorded ones.
513|    - Plain MLX at 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts went from 33 to 57–102 ms per step while recording, with the GPU idle for long stretches. The cause was not found, and its times are not used.
514|    - Xcode's full Metal System Trace template, used first, cost up to 20% and was dropped.
515|  - **One recording of about one second per setting.**
516|    - Bytes per step repeat within 0.5% (two recordings of the same step).
517|    - Step times at 32 requests vary by about ±10% between recordings, so the GB/s use the unrecorded step periods.
518|  - **The counters cover the whole GPU.**
519|    - In clean runs, other programs added under 0.2 GB/s (under 1 MB per step).
520|    - In four runs another program used the GPU just before the window: three plain MLX knock-outs with one request, and one with 32. That work did not carry on into the window, so nothing is subtracted for it.
521|  - **What "read bandwidth" counts.** Apple does not document whether reads served by the GPU's caches are counted. The calibration shows the units, and the experts' 908 MB against 1,416 MB read per pair suggests cache hits are not counted (estimate).
522|  - **Knock-outs and caches.** Removing a piece changes what the rest of the step finds in cache, so changes below about 60 MB at 32 requests are not attributed to a piece.
523|- **Prompts are random tokens**, as in the sweep. The two engines draw them from different generators, so their routing differs slightly: at 32 rows, 40.1 distinct experts per layer in plain MLX against 36.4 in vLLM, in the counted step.
524|
525|## How this was measured
526|
527|The same machine and software as the baseline ([method](../benchmark/method.md)): vLLM 0.32.0, vllm-metal 0.32.0.dev20261028121433 (commit e177b67), mlx 0.32.4 and macOS 15.7.4, with `models/MobileMoE-S-QAT-mlx-bfloat16`.
528|
529|The runs took place on 2026-11-01 between 01:37 EDT and 01:24 EST (Docker's VM quit for 48 minutes in all). The order was plain MLX (14 min), vLLM (20 min), then `repeat_fixes.py`. `lm_head_shapes.py` ran afterwards, with Docker running again.
530|
531|A first attempt on 2026-10-31 ran out of memory. Plain MLX scored all 32 × 1,024 prompt positions at once, 8.4 GB of logits. The harness now runs prompts the way mlx_lm generate does: in chunks of at most 2,048 tokens, scoring only the last position. A one-off check with the float32 model found the same next-token logits as a single pass, to within 0.0001.
532|
533|To reproduce, run from the repo root (about 45 minutes):
534|
535|```bash
536|R=results/runs/<date>-breakdown
537|.venv/bin/python bench/micro/breakdown.py plain $R
538|VLLM_METAL_KV_COMMIT_PROBE=0 .venv/bin/python bench/micro/breakdown.py vllm $R
539|.venv/bin/python bench/micro/repeat_fixes.py plain $R

542|.venv/bin/python bench/micro/breakdown_tables.py $R > $R/tables.md
543|```
544|
545|Drop `VLLM_METAL_KV_COMMIT_PROBE=0` on a machine with memory to spare.

{"content":"# Territory: findings

- **Owner:** explorer-findings
- **Status:** exploring
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:30Z
- **Next:** post inefficiency entries ineff-findings-1..3

## What it does

This territory is the measured evidence, not code: the three findings documents in
`claude/findings/` and the raw breakdown run in
`results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/`. It tells every other explorer what each piece
of the decode step costs in place (kernels, CPU, knock-out savings) so no
inefficiency is claimed without a measured cost. The headline numbers the swarm
builds on: the 1-row step is a chain of 867 kernels where routing+combine cost
1.63 ms of 4.75 ms, and at 32 rows the routed experts cost 14.67 ms of 28.19 ms
while reading 908 MB against the 443 MB they need.

## Checklist

### A. Step periods and the vLLM-vs-plain-MLX gap

- **Callers:** `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md` §1 (lines 101-116); the brief's
  slot costs (§`routing`/`combine`/`experts`) rest on these knock-outs.
- **Callees:** `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` "Step period by mode"
  (lines 14-24) and "Each repeat" (lines 26-52); raw records in `runs-plain.jsonl`,
  `runs-vllm.jsonl` (one record per run).
- **Data:** bare-mode medians of 3 repeats. Plain MLX: 4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms at
  1 / 8 / 32 rows × 128-token prompts, 33.20 ms at 32 × 1024. vLLM: 5.64 / 14.30 /
  30.47 / 39.71 ms. vLLM's extra: +19% / +7% / +8% / +20% (+6.51 ms long-context).
- **Neighbours:** piece B (runner spans) explains the 1-row gap as CPU; piece H
  (attention) explains the long-context gap. Replaces decode-bottlenecks finding 1
  ("5-10%"), which compared different harnesses.
- **Cost:** the whole-step denominators every saving is measured against: 4.75 ms
  at 1 row, 28.19 ms at 32 rows (plain MLX, bare).
- **Invariants:** steady decode steps only (first 5 of 256 dropped); random-token
  prompts, different generators per engine (routing differs slightly: 40.1 vs 36.4
  distinct experts/layer at 32 rows); machine paged heavily throughout (Limits,
  step-breakdown lines 493-497; `machine-*.txt`).

### B. Runner spans: who sets the pace, CPU or GPU

- **Callers:** step-breakdown §2 (lines 117-144); decode-bottlenecks §4
  (lines 135-156) for the profiled submit-call split.
- **Callees:** tables.md "Time per step in each runner span, cpu mode" (lines 54-71)
  and "CPU time per step to build each piece's graph" (lines 73-110).
- **Data:** per-step means over 3 repeats, cpu mode. vLLM schedule: 0.06 / 0.12 /
  0.30 / 0.48 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 / 32-long. Encode (`submit`): plain 2.61 / 3.61 /
  6.02 ms, vLLM 4.10 / 4.70 / 6.46 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows. GPU-wait inside
  `mx.async_eval`: 0.41 ms (vLLM, 1 row) vs 19.39 ms (vLLM, 32 rows).
- **Neighbours:** at 8+ rows the GPU sets the pace (runner work is free); at 1 row
  vLLM is CPU-set (0.41 ms GPU wait; plain MLX has 0.67 ms wait, GPU-set with CPU
  to spare). 1-row vLLM cpu-mode column is an upper bound (instrumentation
  lengthens the step 5.64 -> 7.44 ms).
- **Cost:** scheduler never the problem (0.06-0.30 ms); runner outside the model
  0.5 / 0.9 / 1.6 ms at 1 / 8 / 32 rows; encoding the largest CPU cost (4.10 ms
  vLLM vs 2.61 ms plain at 1 row).
- **Invariants:** cpu-mode 1-row vLLM figures are upper bounds; profiled Python
  figures (decode-bottlenecks §4) overstate Python parts.

### C. Per-piece cost at 1 row: routing+combine beat the expert math

- **Callers:** step-breakdown §3 "With one request" (lines 155-195);
  bottleneck-explained §3 (lines 106-118); brief slot costs (routing 1.02 ms,
  combine 0.61 ms, experts 0.92 ms at 1 row).
- **Callees:** tables.md knock-out tables (lines 320-356: "What removing a piece
  saves", median and fastest-repeat) and "Each piece at 1 row" (lines 358-375);
  kernel counts from tables.md "Kernel operations per step" (lines 112-147).
- **Data:** plain MLX, per step of 20 layers. Routing: 240 kernels, 173 µs CPU,
  saves 1.02 ms (4.3 µs/kernel). Routed experts: 140 kernels, 220 µs CPU, saves
  0.92 ms (6.6 µs/kernel). Combine: 100 kernels, 75 µs CPU, saves 0.61 ms
  (6.1 µs/kernel). Shared expert: 80 kernels, saves 0.51 ms. Output layer: 1
  kernel, saves 0.39 ms (158 GB/s). MoE all: 560 kernels, 2.94 ms. Attention all:
  220 kernels, 1.21 ms.
- **Neighbours:** vLLM 1-row knock-outs are ranges/noise (paging; step-breakdown
  lines 175-176) — use plain MLX at 1 row. Sync-mode GPU times are NOT used
  (sum 5-8x the real step; Limits lines 503-505); only kernel counts come from
  sync mode.
- **Cost:** routing+combine = 340 kernels and 1.63 ms, a third of the 4.75 ms
  step — more than the routed experts' 0.92 ms. Most pieces cost 4-7 µs/kernel.
- **Invariants:** knock-out saving = piece cost where it runs (CPU, GPU or both);
  a faster version gains less than the full saving (Limits lines 507-509).

### D. Per-piece cost at 32 rows: the routed experts take half the step

- **Callers:** step-breakdown §3 "With 32 requests" (lines 196-230);
  bottleneck-explained §4 (lines 120-133); brief (experts 14.67 ms of 28.19 ms).
- **Callees:** tables.md lines 320-356 (knock-outs) and 377-394 ("Each piece at
  32 rows"); both engines agree within 2.5% at 32 rows.
- **Data:** plain MLX, per step. Routed experts: 260 kernels (140 + 120 sort ops:
  60 Gather, 40 ArgSort, 20 FloorDivide — tables.md lines 136-139), 537 µs CPU,
  saves 14.67 ms (52%). Attention all: 5.60 ms (kernel 3.12). Shared expert: 2.90
  ms. Output layer: 2.50 ms. Routing: 1.68 ms. Combine: 0.33 ms. MoE all: 680
  kernels, 17.09 ms (60%).
- **Neighbours:** vLLM output layer saves 5.08 ms vs plain 2.50 ms — unexplained,
  not the kernel (`lm_head_shapes.txt`: 2.351 vs 2.356 ms either layout, same
  logits); at least one vLLM 32-row knock-out removes more than its piece
  (top-level savings sum to 33.3 ms > 30.3 ms step). Use plain MLX figures.
- **Cost:** experts 14.67 ms (52%); attention 5.60 ms (20%); routing bookkeeping
  stops mattering (6%).
- **Invariants:** 32-row savings are not additive (removing a large piece changes
  overlap; replayed outputs change later routing — step-breakdown lines 225,
  507-509).

### E. Derived bandwidth/compute and the fixed cost per kernel

- **Callers:** step-breakdown §3 "Memory bandwidth and compute, piece by piece"
  (lines 231-295); bottleneck-explained §§1-3 (lines 47-118); decode-bottlenecks
  §2 (lines 83-112).
- **Callees:** tables.md "Achieved bandwidth and compute of each piece" (lines
  408-438) and "The whole step's achieved bandwidth and compute" (lines 440-450);
  op mix from tables.md "Operations per step by type" (lines 149-159).
- **Data:** peaks 200 GB/s, 5.2 TFLOP/s. Whole step uses 12-19% of peak bandwidth
  (38 / 29 / 26 / 39 GB/s plain at 1 / 8 / 32 / 32-long), 5.1-8.7x its lower
  bound — overhead-bound in both engines. At 1 row a piece's GB/s follows bytes
  per kernel: output layer 158 (1 kernel, 61.6 MB), shared expert 86, projections
  ~30, routing 4 (240 kernels, 3.7 MB). Kernel count 867 (1 row) / 987 (32 rows)
  plain, 968 / 1088 vLLM; tiny-op chain 6.81 µs/op end to end.
- **Neighbours:** bytes count each weight once and skip activations, so derived
  GB/s are lower bounds on real traffic. GPU counters (runs territory,
  2026-11-02) check them: 1-row reads 193 MB vs 180 MB needed; output layer
  167 GB/s vs derived 158.
- **Cost:** at 5-7 µs/kernel, a kernel reading 0.37 MB cannot exceed 50-75 GB/s;
  at 1 row the limit is the kernel count, not bandwidth.
- **Invariants:** lower bound = max(bytes/200 GB/s, FLOP/5.2 TFLOP/s); 1-row vLLM
  excluded (CPU-set, savings are CPU time).

### F. Expert bytes: per-pair reads, and the grouped kernel that never runs

- **Callers:** bottleneck-explained §4 (lines 135-194); decode-bottlenecks §5
  (lines 158-204); step-breakdown §3 memory-traffic subsection.
- **Callees:** per-layer distinct experts in `runs-plain.jsonl` (`distinct_experts`
  in sync records; e.g. 43,50,45,...,39 at 32 rows, total 802 pairs; means in
  tables.md lines 396-406); MLX `quantized.cpp:2011-2012` rule (`M==1 && B>=16 &&
  sorted && B/E>=4` → grouped needs 240+ pairs = 60+ rows); `switch_layers.py:181`
  (sort from 64 pairs = 16 rows). Byte totals (908 MB read, 443 MB needed) are
  runs-territory counter data (2026-11-02) cited by the findings.
- **Data:** one expert = 3 × 294,912 int4 weights = 0.553 MB (weights 147,456 B +
  scales/offsets 36,864 B per matrix). 32 rows: 2,560 pairs ask 1,416 MB;
  distinct-once needs 443 MB; 908 MB reached memory → 465 MB extra (30% of the
  1,557 MB step reads), cache served the other half of the 973 MB repeat reads.
  Per-pair vs grouped on equal balanced data (chained 20 layers): 5.08→3.82

- **Callers:** bottleneck-explained §6 (lines 223-283); step-breakdown §3 memory

- **Callees:** MLX `quantized.cpp:89-125` (`get_qmv_batch_limit` = 14 rows on

{"content":"# Inefficiency: routing+combine bookkeeping dominates the 1-row step

- **Owner:** explorer-findings
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:35Z
- **Next:** verifier to check the arithmetic against tables.md

## Slot

`routing` + `combine` (the brief's `routing+combine` slot).

## What happens

Routing (cast, router product, sigmoid, bias add, negate, argpartition, gather,
weight normalisation) launches 240 kernels per step and combine (weight, sum, cast
back, add shared) 100 more — 340 of the step's 867 kernels at 1 row
(`results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md`, "Each piece at 1 row", lines
358-375; op mix in "Operations per step by type", lines 149-159). The router
product is the only real math; the rest is selection and weighting bookkeeping
(`third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:217-232`, as split in
step-breakdown "How the step was cut into pieces").

## Cost

Plain MLX, knock-out savings (tables.md "What removing a piece saves", lines
320-356) over bare step periods (4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms):

- **1 row:** 340 kernels. Routing 1.02 ms / 240 = 4.3 µs per kernel; combine
  0.61 ms / 100 = 6.1 µs per kernel. Bytes: routing must read 3.7 MB/step, so
  3.7 MB / 200 GB/s = 19 µs; combine reads activations only. Measured total:
  **1.63 ms of the 4.75 ms step (34%)**.
- **8 rows:** knock-outs did not run at 8 rows (step-breakdown: knock-outs at 1
  and 32 rows only), and the kernel count is identical to 1 row (867, same op
  mix). Estimate by linear interpolation in rows: routing
  1.02 + (1.68 − 1.02) × 7/31 = 1.17 ms; combine
  0.61 + (0.33 − 0.61) × 7/31 = 0.55 ms; total **≈1.72 ms of 13.37 ms (13%)**.
- **32 rows:** routing 1.68 ms / 240 = 7.0 µs per kernel; combine 0.33 ms / 100 =
  3.3 µs per kernel. Measured total: **2.01 ms of the 28.19 ms step (7%)**.

## Kind

Overhead-bound (glossary: far below both limits). Routing moves 2-4 GB/s; combine
reads no weights. The cost is 340 fixed kernel costs plus their CPU encode.

## Spans

`findings` (measured costs), `model` (MoE block code), `quantized-kernels` (the
router product kernel).

## Predicted saving

If each slot fuses to 1 kernel per layer (20 + 20 = 40 kernels vs 340), saving
300 fixed costs per step:

- **1 row:** routing (240 − 20) × 4.3 = 946 µs; combine (100 − 20) × 6.1 =
  488 µs; total **≈1420 µs per step**.
- **8 rows (estimate):** routing 220 × (1.17 ms / 240 = 4.9 µs) = 1078 µs;
  combine 80 × (0.55 ms / 100 = 5.5 µs) = 440 µs; total **≈1500 µs per step**.
- **32 rows:** routing 220 × 7.0 = 1540 µs; combine 80 × 3.3 = 264 µs; total
  **≈1800 µs per step**.

Supporting evidence: compiling the whole 20-layer MoE stack as one function cut
the block 6.02 → 4.27 ms (−29%) at 1 row in the chained test
(decode-bottlenecks §3) — a different measurement (synchronous, includes
build+encode), so an existence proof, not a prediction. Caveats: knock-out
savings include CPU encode, which fusion also cuts (favourable); but a faster
version gains less than the full saving (step-breakdown Limits).

- **Owner:** explorer-findings
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:35Z
- **Next:** verifier to check the arithmetic against tables.md

## Slot

`experts`.

## What happens

Below 60 rows per step MLX runs the per-pair kernel (`gather_qvm`), which handles
each (token, expert) pair on its own and reads the expert's weights once per
pair; the grouped kernel (`gather_qmm_rhs`), which reads each expert once, needs
240+ pairs and never runs in decode (MLX 0.32.4 `quantized.cpp:2011-2012`, via
decode-bottlenecks §5). At 32 rows the 2,560 pairs ask for 1,416 MB while the 802
distinct (layer, expert) pairs need 443 MB (bottleneck-explained §4; per-layer
distinct counts in `runs-plain.jsonl` `distinct_experts`). Sorting from 16 rows
(120 extra sort kernels/step: 60 Gather, 40 ArgSort, 20 FloorDivide — tables.md
lines 136-139) only reorders the per-pair kernel's visits. One expert is
0.553 MB (3 × 294,912 int4 weights + scales/offsets).

## Cost

Plain MLX, knock-out savings (tables.md lines 320-356) over bare steps
(4.75 / 13.37 / 28.19 ms); byte totals from the GPU counters (2026-11-02) as
quoted in the findings:

- **1 row:** 140 kernels × (0.92 ms / 140 = 6.6 µs). Bytes: 51 MB read /
  200 GB/s = 255 µs (44 MB needed → 220 µs). Measured: **0.92 ms of 4.75 ms
  (19%)**, 48 GB/s on needed bytes (24% of peak). Each weight already read once.
- **8 rows:** not measured (no knock-outs, no per-piece counters at 8 rows).
  Rough estimate: cost per pair interpolates 11.5 µs (0.92 ms / 80 pairs at 1
  row) → 5.7 µs (14.67 ms / 2,560 pairs at 32 rows); 640 pairs × ~8 µs ≈
  **≈5.1 ms of 13.37 ms (38%)**. Asked 354 MB, needed 221 MB (20.0 distinct
  experts/layer × 20 × 0.553 MB).
- **32 rows:** 260 kernels. Bytes: 908 MB read / 200 GB/s = 4.54 ms. Measured:
  **14.67 ms of 28.19 ms (52%)**, 62 GB/s (31% of peak). The 465 MB of repeat
  reads that reach memory are 30% of the step's 1,557 MB reads; the cache serves
  the other half of the 973 MB repeat reads.

## Kind

Overhead-bound at all row counts (6% of peak compute, 30 GB/s on needed bytes at
32 rows — far below both limits), with a bandwidth-waste component at 32 rows
(465 MB extra reads). Most of the 14.67 ms is kernel efficiency, not bytes:
908 MB at peak = 4.5 ms, 443 MB at peak = 2.2 ms (bottleneck-explained §4,
estimate).

## Spans

`findings` (measured costs), `quantized-kernels` (gather_qmm kernel choice),
`switch-layers` (pair sorting from 16 rows), `model` (expert call).

## Predicted saving

Basis: the grouped kernel is 25-36% faster on equal balanced data (4-5
pairs/expert): 15.02 → 9.63 ms at 32 rows chained over 20 layers
(decode-bottlenecks §5). Real routing shares less (3.2 pairs/expert at 32 rows,
128/40.1; 2.2 at 16 rows), where the grouped win is untested — so 25% is the
planning figure and 36% the upper end:

- **1 row:** weights already read once; saving comes from fusing 7 kernels/layer
  (brief) toward 1-2: (140 − 40) × 6.6 µs ≈ **660 µs per step**.
- **8 rows (rough estimate):** 25% × ~5.1 ms ≈ **1300 µs per step**; at 1.6
  pairs/expert (32/20.0) the grouped kernel is untested and the gain could be
  near zero — fusion only.
- **32 rows:** 25% × 14.67 ms = **3670 µs per step** (upper 36% ≈ 5280 µs).
  Per layer: 733 µs → save ~183 µs.

## Verdict

{"content":"# Inefficiency: split-K partial-result traffic from 14 rows up

- **Owner:** explorer-findings
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:35Z
- **Next:** verifier to check the arithmetic against the findings

## Slot

Outside the slots (the q, k, v, o projections and the shared expert — no slot
covers them). Posted so the swarm does not mistake this traffic for expert or
attention bytes.

## What happens

From 14 rows up, MLX runs its quantized products split-K: the K dimension is cut
into chunks, each chunk writes its own float32 copy of the output
(`split_k × rows × outputs` numbers), and a second kernel reads them back and
adds them up (`quantized.cpp:1166-1226`, threshold `get_qmv_batch_limit` = 14 on
applegpu_g13s at `:89-125` — all via step-breakdown §3 / bottleneck-explained
§6). At 32 rows split_k is 12/24/24/12 for q/k/v/o and 8/8/16 for the shared
expert's gate/up/down; the buffers total 173 MB per step (23.6 + 15.7 + 15.7 +
23.6 + 31.5 + 31.5 + 31.5 MB). That is why the step writes 3 MB at 1 row and
20-21 MB at 8 rows but 251-266 MB at 32 rows (GPU counters, 2026-11-02, as
quoted in the findings).

## Cost

- **1 row:** split-K off. Writes 3 MB/step. Cost **0**.

1|# Inefficiency: each (token, expert) pair runs its own qvm grid at ~1/3 peak bandwidth
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-quantized-kernels
4|- **Status:** open
5|- **Version:** 1
6|- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:45Z
7|- **Next:** verifier to confirm dispatch lines and the GB/s arithmetic
8|
9|## Slot
10|
11|`experts`
12|
13|## What happens
14|
15|Every routed-expert product in decode runs `affine_gather_qvm`
16|(`quantized.h:2355-2416` + `qvm_impl`, `:1222-1330`): `M=1` rules out the matrix
17|path and `B/E<=2.1 < 4` rules out the rhs batched path forever at `rows<=32`
18|(`quantized.cpp:2005-2093 @v0.32.4`; full proof in
19|`territory-quantized-kernels.md` section A). Consequences, all in this kernel:
20|
21|1. Each pair re-reads its expert's full weights through its own grid (gate/up 6
22|   threadgroups, down 12, 64 threads each). At 32 rows, 128 grids per product
23|   stream 908 MB for 443 MB of distinct experts.
24|2. Lanes read strided: consecutive lanes sit `out_vec_size_w` apart (gate: 192 B
25|   stride for 16 B loads, `qvm_impl:1262`), scales `out_vec_size_g` apart (12
26|   elements, 2 B used per 24 B stride, `:1263-1264`) — poor DRAM coalescing.
27|3. Each pair's `x` row is re-read 12x per product (every tile's 2 simdgroups
28|   stream the full K row, `:1275-1287`): ~55 KB x per pair vs 3.75 KB needed,
29|   ~131 MB/step excess at 32 rows, inside the 908 MB.
30|4. At 1 row the grids are 24/24/48 threadgroups (~1.5-3K threads, ~5-10% of the
31|   16-core GPU's slots): occupancy-starved.
32|
33|## Cost
34|
35|Per decode step, plain MLX (GPU counters
36|`results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md:17-18`, knock-outs
37|`results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md:210-213,259-262`):
38|
39|- 1 row: 60 GatherQMM launches x ~6 us (`step-breakdown.md:179-185`: routed
40|  experts 140 kernels / 0.92 ms) ~ 0.36 ms; 51 MB read in 0.92 ms = 55 GB/s.
41|- 8 rows: no serving knock-out; bytes modelled 383 MB/pair-traffic
42|  (540 KB weights + 55 KB x per pair x 32 pairs x 20 layers); micro chained
43|  products 5.08 ms per 20 layers unsorted (`moe_parts.txt:6`) = ~75 GB/s.
44|- 32 rows: 908 MB read in 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step = 62 GB/s, 31% of peak.
45|
46|## Kind
47|
48|Overhead-bound at 1 row (51 MB needs 0.26 ms at peak; measured 0.92 ms; tiny
49|grids); bandwidth-bound at low efficiency at 8/32 rows (streaming kernel at
50|~1/3 peak: arithmetic intensity ~3 FLOP/B << ridge point 26, `GLOSSARY.md`).
51|
52|## Spans
53|
54|`quantized-kernels` (kernel + dispatch) -> slot `experts`. Measurements shared
55|with `runs`; sort interaction with `switch-layers`.
56|
57|## Predicted saving
58|
59|A fused kernel batching same-expert pairs with coalesced reads (the design
60|`gather_qmm_rhs` was built for but never fires) runs the same traffic at a
61|normal streaming rate, ~150 GB/s (the output layer hits 158 GB/s where it sits,
62|`step-breakdown.md:193-195`). Same bytes at 150 GB/s, per decode step:
63|
64|- 1 row: 51 MB: 0.92 - 0.34 = 0.58, minus ~0.1 ms residual (4 pairs stay small)
65|  = **0.5 ms**.
66|- 8 rows: 383 MB: 5.08 - 2.55 = **2.5 ms** (micro baseline, caveat below).
67|- 32 rows: 908 MB: 14.67 - 6.05 = **8.6 ms**.
68|
69|Overlap: complementary to `ineff-runs-1` (removes 465 MB of the 908 for 2.3 ms
70|at peak; combined ideal 443 MB @150 ~ 3.0 ms, total prize ~11.5 ms, consistent).
71|At 8 rows overlaps `ineff-runs-3` (its 1.3 ms sorting prize is part of this
72|2.5 ms via locality; net-new ~1.2 ms). Launch overhead shared with
73|`ineff-quantized-kernels-2` (~0.2 ms, count once).
74|Caveat at 8 rows: micro used 8 experts and chained calls, not serving's
75|distinct count and glue; serving prize may differ (same caveat as `ineff-runs-3`).
76|
77|## Verdict
78|
79|(verifier to write)

1|# Inefficiency: sort glue costs 6 kernels/layer from 16 rows, for locality only
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-switch-layers
4|- **Status:** open
5|- **Version:** 1
6|- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:30Z
7|- **Next:** verifier to confirm kernel inventory and the B/E>=4 gate
8|
9|## Slot
10|
11|`experts`
12|
13|## What happens
14|
15|When `indices.size >= 64` (`switch_layers.py:181`), i.e. 16+ decode rows,
16|`SwitchGLU` sorts the 4·rows pairs by expert (`_gather_sort`, `:12-17`) and
17|un-sorts afterwards (`_scatter_unsort`, `:20-24`). Per layer that is 2 ArgSort
18|(`order`, and a second full sort for `inv_order`), 1 FloorDivide (`order // M`),
19|and 3 Gathers (sorted x, sorted idx, unsort) — 6 kernels/layer, 120/step
20|(`results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md:136`: Gather 60, ArgSort 40,
21|FloorDivide 20; the 867→987 op jump at 32 rows).
22|
23|The sort cannot change MLX's kernel choice in decode: the grouped path needs
24|`B/E >= 4` (`quantized.cpp:2012`, v0.32.4), i.e. 240+ pairs at E=60 = 60+ rows,
25|so every decode row count runs the per-pair `gather_qvm` kernel regardless
26|(see `territory-switch-layers.md` §G). Its only function in serving is cache
27|locality within that kernel (sorted serving reads 908 MB vs the 1416 MB
28|per-pair model — caches serve a third).
29|
30|## Cost
31|
32|Per decode step (plain MLX, 128-token prompts):
33|
34|- 1 row: no sort runs (4 pairs < 64) — 0 kernels, 0 ms.
35|- 8 rows: no sort runs (32 pairs < 64) — 0 kernels, 0 ms.
36|- 32 rows: 120 kernels/step, ~5 of the 6 per layer on the critical chain
37|  (`inv_order`'s argsort overlaps the products). 5 × 6.81 µs × 20 layers
38|  = 0.68 ms ≈ 0.7 ms (fixed-cost unit from
39|  `results/runs/2026-10-30-micro/step_parts.txt`). Index/activation traffic is
40|  ~8 MB/step ≈ 0.04 ms at peak — negligible. No isolated knock-out; contained
41|  in the experts 14.67 ms (`step-breakdown.md:211`). CPU record for the experts
42|  glue rises 128 → 399 µs/step from 1 to 32 rows (`tables.md:99`).
43|
44|## Kind
45|
46|Overhead-bound: ~0.7 ms of fixed kernel costs moving ~8 MB.
47|
48|## Spans
49|
50|`switch-layers`, `quantized-kernels` (kernel fixed costs), `runs` (inventory).
51|
52|## Predicted saving
53|
54|Standalone removal would *lose* time (unsorted pairs lose the locality that
55|keeps a third of repeat reads in cache — size unmeasured in serving). The
56|saving is realizable only inside a fused grouped `experts` kernel that needs
57|no sort: then the full ~0.7 ms at 32 rows plus the 8 MB traffic go, jointly
58|with `ineff-runs-1` and `ineff-switch-layers-2` (one fix; savings do not add):
59|
60|- 1 row: 0.0 ms (no sort runs).
61|- 8 rows: 0.0 ms (no sort runs).
62|- 32 rows: ≈ 0.7 ms (100 on-chain kernels × 6.81 µs).
63|
64|## Verdict
65|
66|(verifier to write)

1|# Inefficiency: gate/up/down products and activation unfused
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-switch-layers

13|## What happens

15|Each layer launches three separate `mx.gather_qmm` kernels (up, gate, down;
16|`switch_layers.py:188-194` via `mobilemoe.py:172-184`) plus one compiled
17|silu-mul activation kernel (`activations.py:9-11`, `tables.md:136,141`): 4
18|on-chain kernels/layer, 80/step at every row count, plus 3 off-chain default
19|`Arange` kernels/layer (60/step, measured ~free — `step-breakdown.md:438-463`).
20|Between them the gate, up and silu-mul bf16 outputs are written to memory and
21|re-read: at 32 rows 3 × [128,1,384] bf16 = 0.29 MB/layer = 5.9 MB/step; at 1
22|row 3 × [4,1,384] = 9 KB/layer. One fused kernel could do all three products
23|and the activation in registers/shared memory.

26|

28|
29|- 1 row: experts knock-out 0.92 ms for 140 kernels = 6.6 µs each
30|  (`step-breakdown.md:170,182`). Fixed-cost share of the 4 fusable kernels:
31|  4 × 6.81 µs × 20 = 0.54 ms; intermediates 0.2 MB ≈ 0.00 ms.
32|- 8 rows: same structure as 1 row (no sort; 867 ops, `tables.md:153`). No
33|  knock-out at 8 rows; fixed-cost share again ≈ 0.54 ms (estimate, same kernels).
34|- 32 rows: experts knock-out 14.67 ms (`step-breakdown.md:211`). Fixed-cost
35|  share of the 4 ≈ 0.54 ms; intermediates 5.9 MB ≈ 0.03 ms at peak. The rest of
36|  the 14.67 ms is per-pair weight reads (`ineff-runs-1`) and small-kernel
37|  efficiency, not this entry.
38|
39|## Kind
40|
41|Overhead-bound: 80 on-chain kernels/step doing 4 launches where 1 suffices.
42|
43|## Spans
44|
45|`switch-layers`, `quantized-kernels`.
46|
47|## Predicted saving
48|
49|Fusing the 3 products + activation into one kernel (keeping per-pair reads —
50|grouping is `ineff-runs-1`'s prize; one combined fix, savings do not add):
51|
52|- 1 row: 3 launches/layer saved ≈ 3 × 6.81 µs × 20 = 0.4 ms.
53|- 8 rows: ≈ 0.4 ms (same kernel structure; estimate).
54|- 32 rows: ≈ 0.4 ms fixed costs + 5.9 MB intermediate traffic (0.03 ms at
55|  peak); larger threadgroups should also lift efficiency — unquantified.
56|
57|A fused kernel must keep the boundary: fp32 accumulation + bf16 rounding per
58|product, silu-mul on bf16 values rounded to bf16 before the down product
59|(brief §experts).

62|

Read text file `.agents/skills/muse-round/SKILL.md`.
1|---
2|name: muse-round
3|description: Run one Muse Spark round on the MobileMoE-S decode kernels as a swarm. Explorers map the code and measurements into a shared analysis; then competing builders write and grade fused Metal kernels for the top inefficiencies. Both phases are tracked in shared documents.
4|---
5|
6|# One Muse Spark round: a swarm explores, then builds
7|
8|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed on main and tagged `muse-code-era` before the first Muse Code session; each later version is committed before the round that uses it. [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
9|
10|**Skill version 3.** This file, the role cards and tracking.md are versioned together; [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) lists every version. Each round records the version it ran (see *Versions* in tracking.md).
11|
12|You are Muse Spark, the **lead** of a Muse Code session in your own worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. `claude/muse-agent-brief.md` fixes the task, the four slots, the tools and limits, the grader command and the pass criteria (G1, G2). Two ADRs change it in four ways:
13|
14|1. **Harness** ([ADR 0006](../../../claude/adr/0006-muse-spark-in-muse-code.md)). You are a Muse Code session, not a Claude Code one. Muse Code adds no trailer, so you write it on every commit yourself (see *Commits*).
15|2. **No attempt limit and no stop rule** (ADR 0006). You decide when a slot is done. Every graded attempt is committed, so the history shows every try.
16|3. **A swarm** ([ADR 0007](../../../claude/adr/0007-muse-spark-swarm.md)). Helpers explore and build; you coordinate and commit.
17|4. **Files** (ADR 0007). `muse-spark/exploration/` and `muse-spark/implementation/` hold the round's shared documents, and they replace `strategy.md`. Kernels and `summary.md` stay where the brief puts them.
18|
19|The rest of the brief stands. The goal is unchanged: kernels that pass G1 and G2 and beat the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 rows, faster because they remove a cause you can name.
20|
21|## The swarm
22|
23|| Role | Name | Task | Card |
24||---|---|---|---|
25|| **Lead** (you) | | Start the helpers, keep the two READMEs, settle clashes, commit | this file |
26|| **Explorer** | `explorer-<territory>` | Map one territory into entries, and find where it loses time | [explorer.md](explorer.md) |
27|| **Verifier** | `verifier` | Check every inefficiency against its sources | [verifier.md](verifier.md) |
28|| **Builder** | `builder-<n>-<letter>` | Write and grade one solution for one hypothesis: one attempt | [builder.md](builder.md) |
29|| **Boundary agent** | `boundary-<n>` | Write what a hypothesis's solution must keep identical, and check passing attempts against it | [boundary.md](boundary.md) |
30|
31|You don't explore, build or grade yourself. Start each helper with a prompt of this shape:
32|
33|> You are `<name>`, a `<role>` in this round's swarm. Read `.agents/skills/muse-round/<card>` and `.agents/skills/muse-round/tracking.md`, then: `<task>`.
34|
35|[tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the shared documents (the two phase folders, their READMEs, entries and logs) and the rules every agent keeps. Read it before starting anyone. Up to 12 agents run at once, you included.
36|
37|**A checkpoint** is what you do each time a helper returns, and whenever the log shows something to settle:
38|1. **Read the log.** Read the phase log since your last checkpoint.
39|2. **Settle clashes.** When two entries describe one cause, keep the fuller one and set the other's status to `superseded by <entry>`. When two helpers work on one item, redirect one of them (`subagent_send_message`). Log what you decided.
40|3. **Refresh the tracker.** Update the phase README's tracker table, and raise the version of each hypothesis entry that changed.
41|4. **Raise the version.** Raise the phase README to its next version, and add its line to `## Versions`, naming the entries that changed and their versions (see *Versions* in tracking.md).
42|5. **Commit** the phase folder, plus any attempt that came back, as that version (see *Commits*).
43|
44|## The round
45|
46|### 0. Find where you are
47|
48|- Run `git log --oneline main -1`, then `git log --oneline --grep '^Muse Spark:' muse-code-era..HEAD`, which lists your earlier commits.
49|- **Round number:** `claude/findings/muse-round-<N>.md` holds Claude's measurement of round N, run after merging your branch. This round is one more than the highest N. With no such file, it is round 1.
50|- From round 2 on, read the newest of those files first. It has the G3 results of your attempts, and it is the first evidence for this round. The phase folders already exist:
51|  - explorers add a `## Round N` section to their entries rather than starting over;
52|  - you start explorers only for the territories the G3 results reopen;
53|  - the logs carry on.
54|- Read the brief.
55|
56|Done when you can name the round number, your committed attempts per slot, and the latest G3 results, if any.
57|
58|### 1. Exploration
59|
60|1. **Set up the folder.** Write `muse-spark/exploration/README.md` with a heading, its version line (v1, with skill version 3), the tracker (one row per territory) and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`. From round 2 on, the README carries on from its last version.
61|2. **Start the explorers and the verifier,** all at once, with these starting territories:
62|
63|   | Territory | Covers |
64|   |---|---|
65|   | `model` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py`: the decoder layer, `MoE.__call__` and everything around the slots |
66|   | `switch-layers` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/switch_layers.py`: the routed experts' path, `gather_qmm`, the sort from 16 rows |
67|   | `quantized-kernels` | `quantized.h` and `quantized_utils.h` in `.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/`: the `affine_gather_*` kernels behind `gather_qmm` |
68|   | `other-kernels` | the other Metal kernels in the same folder that the routing and combine slots launch: sort, softmax, reductions, elementwise, copies |
69|   | `vllm-metal` | `third_party/vllm-metal/vllm_metal/`: how the engine runs a decode step around the model |
70|   | `grader` | `bench/grader/`: the slot interface, what G1, G2 and the piece timing measure, and so the boundary every solution keeps |
71|   | `findings` | `claude/findings/` and `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/` |
72|   | `runs` | `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/`, `2026-10-29-baseline/` and `2026-10-30-micro/` |
73|
74|3. **Refocus as costs show up.** When an entry shows that one file holds most of a territory's cost, split it off as a territory of its own, with its own explorer. Merge or close a territory that turns out to hold nothing, and add one when an inefficiency points somewhere no one covers. Log each change and update the tracker.
75|4. **Checkpoint** each time a helper returns.
76|
77|**Done** when every territory entry is `done`, the verifier has returned, and every inefficiency is `confirmed`, `refuted` or `superseded`.
78|
79|### 2. The analysis
80|
81|Write the final `muse-spark/exploration/README.md`. It is the round's report on the code, for this round's builders and for future improvements:
82|
83|- **Tracker:** the final table.
84|- **Context:** the decode step, the MoE block and its slots, and what the measurements say about where the time goes.
85|- **Territory map:** how the territories feed each other. For each territory: what it receives, what it passes on, and its measured cost.
86|- **Inefficiencies, ranked:**
87|  - the confirmed ones inside the slots, ranked by predicted saving as a share of the decode step, averaged over 1, 8 and 32 rows;
88|  - each with its cost, kind and entry;
89|  - Claude's findings marked as Claude's, and the swarm's own reading marked as yours.
90|- **Recommendations:** the confirmed inefficiencies outside the slots, with their evidence. They're for surucuonur's team.
91|- **Refuted claims,** in one line each, so no one chases them again.
92|- **Files read:** links to each territory entry's list.
93|
94|From round 2 on, add a `## Round N` section: what the G3 results confirm, contradict or reveal.
95|
96|Commit it. **Done** when every ranked item links a confirmed entry and every number in the README has its source.
97|
98|### 3. Implementation
99|
100|Take the ranked inefficiencies in order, at most two at a time, in different slots so their attempts never touch. Write `muse-spark/implementation/README.md` with a heading, its version line, the tracker and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`. For each hypothesis:
101|
102|1. **Open the hypothesis.** Write `muse-spark/implementation/hyp-<n>-<slug>.md`, with status `boundary`, the inefficiency and the slot. Add its tracker row and log it.
103|2. **Draw its boundary.** Start `boundary-<n>` to write the boundary, and wait for it.
104|3. **Compete.**
105|   - Set the status to `building`.
106|   - Start 2 or 3 builders, `builder-<n>-a`, `-b` and `-c`. Give each a different direction drawn from the analysis: for example, fusing kernels, reading each weight byte once, or a different threadgroup shape.
107|4. **Collect.** Each time a builder returns:
108|   - checkpoint, committing its attempt folder with the hypothesis entry, the README and the log;
109|   - if the attempt passed G2, start `boundary-<n>` to check it.
110|5. **Harden.**
111|   - Pick the best attempt: it passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, and it is the fastest against the compiled reference across the three row counts.
112|   - Set the status to `hardening`, and start a builder for that attempt's next single change.
113|   - Repeat while the attempt still has a cause you can name and remove.
114|6. **Close.**
115|   - **`ready`:** the best attempt passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, and beats the compiled reference at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and you can name no further change worth making. Write the **Decision**: the attempt, why it is best, and what G3 should show.
116|   - **`dropped`:** say why.
117|
118|Then open the next-ranked inefficiency. **Done** when no confirmed inefficiency is left that you judge will pay. Write why in the implementation README.
119|
120|### 4. Finish
121|
122|1. **The implementation README:** the final tracker, one paragraph per hypothesis, and a **Ready to test** section. It names the attempt per slot that goes to G3, and the change in decode step period you expect at 1, 8 and 32 requests, with how you worked it out.
123|2. **The exploration README:** add *What building taught*, the analysis corrected by what the attempts showed.
124|3. **`muse-spark/summary.md`:** add a `## Round N` section with:
125|   - the skill version this round ran, and the final versions of both READMEs;
126|   - the final attempt per slot;
127|   - the number of graded attempts per slot, this round and in total;
128|   - the expected G3 change;
129|   - what you'd try next;
130|   - your recommendations outside the slots.
131|4. **Commit,** then reply with this round's commits and the words "Round N finished".
132|
133|## Your own rules
134|
135|- **Writes:**
136|  - you write the two READMEs, the hypothesis entries' status blocks and decisions, and `summary.md`;
137|  - every helper writes only what its card names;
138|  - all of it stays in `muse-spark/`, and a commit outside it is refused.
139|- **G3 and vLLM belong to surucuonur's team,** who run them after merging your branch.
140|- **The rules every agent keeps** are in tracking.md.
141|
142|## Commits
143|
144|You are the only agent that commits. Commit only on `muse-agent`.
145|- **What to add:** the phase folders that exist so far (only `exploration` until implementation starts) and the attempt folders that came back. An attempt another builder is still writing waits for its own commit. An entry that is mid-edit is committed as it stands, and finished in a later commit.
146|- **The message:**
147|  - a checkpoint's subject is `Muse Spark: <phase> v<N>: <what changed>`, the version it records;
148|  - other commits start with `Muse Spark:`;
149|  - every message ends with this exact trailer.
150|
151|```bash
152|git add muse-spark/exploration muse-spark/implementation muse-spark/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>
153|git commit -m "Muse Spark: implementation v4: experts attempt 3 graded, passes G2" \
154|  -m "Co-Authored-By: Muse Spark (Meta Model API) <muse-spark@meta-model-api.invalid>"
155|```
156|
157|Use no other co-author. The hooks refuse a commit without this trailer, a commit outside `muse-spark/`, and any merge. Push, merge, rebase, git config and hook skipping stay with surucuonur.

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write a faster MobileMoE-S decode kernel
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
12|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
13|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
14|
15|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
16|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
17|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
18|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
19|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
20|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
21|
22|## The slots
23|
24|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the step: 1 to 32 in decode. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
25|
26|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
27|
28|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
29|
30|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
31||---|---|---|---|
32|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
33|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
34|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
35|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
36|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
37|
38|Reference:
39|
40|```python
41|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
42|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
43|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
44|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
45|```
46|
47|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
48|
49|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
50|
51|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
52||---|---|---|---|
53|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
54|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
55|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
56|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
57|
58|Reference:
59|
60|```python
61|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
62|```
63|
64|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
65|
66|### `routing+combine`
67|
68|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
69|
70|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
71|
72|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
73||---|---|---|---|
74|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
75|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
76|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
77|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
78|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
79|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
80|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
81|
82|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
83|
84|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
85|
86|```python
87|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
88|```
89|
90|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
91|
92|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
93|

1|# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.
6|
7|## Hardware limits
8|
9|**Peak bandwidth**:
10|The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
11|_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed
12|
13|**Peak compute**:
14|The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
15|_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)
16|
17|**Achieved bandwidth**:
18|The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
19|_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)
20|
21|**Arithmetic intensity**:
22|Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
23|_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio
24|
25|**Ridge point**:
26|The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.
27|
28|**Roofline**:
29|The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.
30|
31|## Bottlenecks and fixes
32|
33|**Bandwidth-bound**:
34|A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.
35|
36|**Compute-bound**:
37|A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.
38|
39|**Overhead-bound**:
40|A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
41|_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)
42|
43|**Bottleneck**:
44|The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
45|_Avoid_: issue, slowness
46|
47|**Kernel**:
48|One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
49|_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)
50|
51|**Occupancy**:
52|The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
53|_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)
54|
55|**Knock-out**:
56|A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
57|_Avoid_: ablation
58|
59|**Baseline**:
60|The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.
61|
62|**Fix**:
63|One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
64|_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak
65|
66|## Inference
67|
68|**Prefill**:
69|Processing a request's whole prompt in one pass before any token is generated.
70|
71|**Decode step**:
72|One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.
73|
74|**Decode rows**:
75|The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
76|_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency
77|
78|**Client concurrency**:
79|The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.
80|_Avoid_: batch size
81|
82|## Mixture of experts
83|
84|**Expert**:
85|One of the interchangeable feed-forward blocks in a layer; MobileMoE-S has 60 routed experts per layer.
86|
87|**Active experts**:
88|The experts the router picks for one token in one layer (4 for MobileMoE-S).
89|_Avoid_: selected experts, top-k experts
90|
91|**Distinct experts**:
92|The number of different experts used by all decode rows together in one layer during one decode step; it decides how much expert weight data the step must read.
93|_Avoid_: unique experts, expert coverage
94|
95|## Models
96|
97|**MobileMoE-S**:
98|Meta's smallest on-device mixture-of-experts model (about 1.3B parameters in total, about 272M used per token), studied here in its SFT (full-precision) and QAT (int4) variants.
99|
100|**Muse Spark**:
101|Meta's hosted model. In this project it chooses which pieces of the decode step to replace and writes their kernels, working in its own Muse Spark session; it is never the model under study.
102|
103|**Muse Code**:
104|Meta's own coding agent for the terminal, built on Muse Spark; the only program in which Muse Spark does its work in this project.
105|_Avoid_: Muse CLI, Meta Code
106|
107|**Muse Spark session**:
108|A Muse Code session in which Muse Spark writes every turn, the lead's and every helper's, kept apart from Claude's work by its own branch, folder and commit trailer.
109|_Avoid_: guardrail (for the session itself), Meta mode
110|
111|## Muse Spark's work
112|
113|**Slot**:
114|One replaceable piece of the mixture-of-experts block (routing, combine, or the routed experts), with fixed inputs and outputs, that Muse Spark may replace with its own kernels.
115|_Avoid_: target (that is a slot Muse Spark has chosen), module
116|
117|**Round**:
118|One Muse Spark session in which a swarm explores and then builds, followed by Claude's independent measurement of what it produced.
119|_Avoid_: iteration, cycle
120|
121|**Swarm**:
122|All the agents of one round, the lead and its helpers, working toward one goal through shared documents that each of them reads and adds to.
123|_Avoid_: team, crew
124|
125|**Lead agent**:
126|The one agent of a swarm that starts the helpers, keeps the shared documents current, settles clashes and commits; it neither explores nor grades.
127|_Avoid_: orchestrator, main agent
128|
129|**Helper agent**:
130|An agent the lead starts: an explorer, the verifier, a builder or a boundary agent. It reports back and never commits.
131|_Avoid_: worker, subagent (when the role matters, not the mechanism)
132|
133|**Reminder agent**:
134|One of Muse Code's own background agents, which watch the lead's progress and may nudge it, for example to check a claim before it says it is done; Muse Spark writes their turns too, but they take no part in the work.
135|_Avoid_: helper (that is one the lead starts)
136|
137|**Exploration phase**:
138|The first part of a round, in which explorers map the code and the measurements and find where the decode step loses time.
139|
140|**Implementation phase**:
141|The second part of a round, in which builders write and grade solutions to the confirmed inefficiencies.
142|_Avoid_: hypothesis phase
143|
144|**Territory**:
145|The part of the code or the measurements that one explorer covers: a module, a single important file, or a measurement document.
146|_Avoid_: area, lens
147|
148|**Analysis**:
149|The swarm's shared account of the code, written during exploration: the context, how the territories feed each other, and the ranked inefficiencies, each with its cost and sources.
150|_Avoid_: diagnosis, findings (those are Claude's)
151|
152|**Inefficiency**:
153|One cause of lost time in the decode step: where it is in the code, what it costs, and what removing it should save. It is confirmed or refuted against its sources before anyone builds on it.
154|_Avoid_: issue, bottleneck (that is the single largest cause)
155|
156|**Hypothesis**:
157|A proposed solution to one inefficiency: the slot it replaces, the boundary it keeps and the saving it predicts, tested by competing attempts.
158|_Avoid_: strategy, plan
159|
160|**Boundary**:
161|What a solution must keep identical so that the steps before and after its slot work exactly as before: the slot's inputs and outputs, their dtypes, and the rounding points.
162|_Avoid_: interface (unqualified), contract
163|
164|**Attempt**:
165|A solution a builder has graded and the lead has committed; attempts for a slot are numbered in order and have no limit.
166|_Avoid_: try, submission, draft

text:
Extracting baseline roofline metrics from summary tables to draft territory-runs status and checklist.

Analyzing CPU submit overhead and MoE kernel costs to identify sorted-flag and compilation impacts.

Quantifying kernel-launch and weight re-read overheads from GPU counters to prioritize inefficiencies.
The three run folders are mapped. Now I'll write the territory entry and inefficiency posts.

tool_calls.args:
{"content":"# Territory: runs

- **Owner:** explorer-runs
- **Status:** exploring
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:20:00Z
- **Next:** post inefficiency entries from the knock-out and micro tables

## What it does

This territory is the measurements, not the code: the three run folders that say where each decode step's time and bytes go. The baseline roofline sets the step budget, the micro tables split the MoE block and count the fixed per-kernel cost, and the GPU-counter tables give achieved bandwidth, occupancy, and per-piece knock-out costs.

## Checklist

### results/runs/2026-10-29-baseline/summary.md (roofline table)

- **Callers:** produced by `bench/roofline.py` from the timed/experts client runs in the same folder; consumed by `claude/findings/` and the brief's slot costs.
- **Callees:** none (a table).
- **Data:** one row per (input_len, concurrency): step ms median with run-median range, submit call ms, submit CPU ms, decode tok/s, distinct experts/layer, MB read/step, GB/s, % of peak, FLOP/byte, min ms at peak. Key rows (in128): c1: 5.49 ms, 32.6 GB/s (16.3%), 3.14 FLOP/byte, 4.0 experts; c8: 14.51 ms, 26.8 GB/s (13.4%), 11.55 FLOP/byte, 19.6 experts; c32: 30.04 ms, 24.0 GB/s (12.0%), 24.93 FLOP/byte, 38.2 experts.
- **Neighbours:** before it, the raw `steps-timed.jsonl`/`runs.json`; after it, the findings that cite it. A replacement reading must keep the same workload (128-token prompts, steady decode steps).
- **Cost:** the step itself: 5.49 ms at c1, 14.51 ms at c8, 30.04 ms at c32 (in128). Submit call ms is nearly the whole step (5.16/5.49 at c1; 29.23/30.04 at c32); submit CPU ms is 4.73 at c1 and 6.89 at c32.
- **Invariants:** steady decode steps only; medians over runs; concurrency caps decode rows but decode rows are what matter (see `steps-timed.jsonl` `rows` field).

### results/runs/2026-10-29-baseline/roofline.json, runs.json, steps-*.jsonl, meta.json

- **Callers:** `summary.md` is generated from these.
- **Callees:** none.
- **Data:** `roofline.json`: per-point step ms, bytes split (every_step 67.6 MB, output 61.6 MB, experts, cache, embedding), FLOPs, achieved GB/s, arithmetic intensity. `meta.json`: M1 Pro, 16 GB, MLX 0.32.4, model MobileMoE-S-QAT-mlx-bfloat16. `steps-timed.jsonl`: per-step build_ms, build_cpu_ms, rows, ctx.
- **Neighbours:** raw material behind the summary table.
- **Cost:** same step budget as above; `roofline.json` costs block gives expert_bytes 552,960 B and cache_bytes_per_token 20,480 B.
- **Invariants:** same workload as the summary.

### results/runs/2026-10-30-micro/step_parts.txt

- **Callers:** microbenchmark script output; feeds the fixed-cost-per-kernel claim.
- **Callees:** none.
- **Data:** tiny dependent op 6.81 µs each (the fixed cost of one small kernel); output layer 0.931 ms at R=1 (66 GB/s) and 2.644 ms at R=32 (23 GB/s); pipelined decode step R=1: 5.04 ms, R=8: 13.85 ms, R=32: 28.91 ms; graph build CPU ~1.0–1.3 ms.
- **Neighbours:** `step_repeats.txt` (medians 4.98 / 13.62 / 28.73 ms) confirms the pipelined step times.
- **Cost:** the fixed ~6.8 µs per tiny kernel is the unit every kernel-count saving multiplies.
- **Invariants:** plain MLX engine, chained eval; repeats in `step_repeats.txt` show ±5% spread.

### results/runs/2026-10-30-micro/moe_parts.txt

- **Callers:** feeds the experts/sort/combine cost split.
- **Callees:** none.
- **Data (ms per 20 layers):** R=1: moe 6.02, moe_compiled 4.27, experts 3.64, shared 1.85, attn_proj 1.08; experts at peak 0.22 ms; per-pair reads 44 MB. R=32: moe 21.56, moe_compiled 20.51, experts 16.60, shared 3.89; experts at peak 2.64 ms; per-pair reads 1416 MB. Kernel A/B sort experiment: rows 32, ours sorted=False 15.02 ms vs sorted=True 9.63 ms per 20 layers; rows 8: 5.08 vs 3.82; rows 16: 8.12 vs 5.65.
- **Neighbours:** `step_parts.txt` gives the whole step these pieces sit in; the gpu-counters knock-out table gives the independent per-piece check.
- **Cost:** experts is ~16.6/21.6 of the MoE block at R=32; sorting pairs by expert saves ~36% of experts time at rows 32 (15.02 → 9.63) and ~25% at rows 8 (5.08 → 3.82).
- **Invariants:** one layer's ops chained ×20; distinct/layer differs from serving (47.8 at R=32 here vs 38.2 in baseline).

### results/runs/2026-10-30-micro/attention_heads.txt

- **Callers:** feeds the attention K/V re-read claim (outside the slots).
- **Callees:** none.
- **Data (µs/layer):** rows 32, ctx 1152: 12q/4kv 568.7 (66.4 GB/s on unique K/V) vs 4q/4kv 247.1 (152.8 GB/s) — same K/V bytes, ~2.3× the time with 3× the query heads. Rows 1, ctx 256: 26.0 vs 18.7 µs/layer.
- **Neighbours:** the knock-out table's attn_kernel row (saves 3.12 ms at 32 rows) bounds the total attention prize.
- **Cost:** the extra query heads re-read K/V instead of sharing it.
- **Invariants:** per_token kernels; ctx 1152 rows are the high-ctx case, above the baseline's mean ctx.

### results/runs/2026-10-30-micro/step-primitives.txt, step_cpu.txt, profile_submit.log, machine.txt, step.dot

- **Callees:** none.

{"content":"# Inefficiency: experts re-reads expert weights per (token, expert) pair

- **Owner:** explorer-runs
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-03T21:25:00Z
- **Next:** verifier to confirm against the knock-out table

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

Each (token, expert) pair's `gather_qmm` reads that expert's gate/up/down weights afresh, so popular experts are re-read once per pair instead of once per step. The knock-out table (`results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`, "Each piece" rows) shows knocking out experts saves 908 MB of reads per step at 32 rows while the model must read only 443 MB for the distinct experts (per-pair model: 1416 MB). At 1 row the two agree (51 vs 44 MB) because all 4 pairs use distinct experts. Mechanism belongs to the switch-layers / quantized-kernels territories; this entry is the measurement.

## Cost

At 1, 8 and 32 rows, per decode step (plain MLX, 128-token prompts):

- 1 row: experts costs 0.92 ms (knock-out, unrecorded) and reads 51 MB vs 44 MB must-read — excess 7 MB.
- 8 rows: no knock-out row; the whole step reads 685 MB vs 393 MB must-read (whole-step table), so the step-wide excess is 292 MB, of which experts is the largest piece by the r1/r32 pattern.
- 32 rows: experts costs 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step and reads 908 MB vs 443 MB must-read — excess 465 MB. Micro corroboration (`results/runs/2026-10-30-micro/moe_parts.txt`): experts 16.60 ms per 20 layers at R=32 vs 2.64 ms at peak bandwidth for the same bytes.

## Kind

Bandwidth-bound: the excess is bytes re-read, ~2× the necessary expert traffic at 32 rows. (The remaining ~12 ms of the 14.67 is kernel overhead and the necessary traffic, owned by the kernel territories.)

## Spans

`runs`, `switch-layers`, `quantized-kernels`

## Predicted saving

Excess bytes removed ÷ peak bandwidth (200 GB/s), per decode step:

- 1 row: 7 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = 0.04 ms ≈ 0.0 ms (nothing lost to re-read at 1 row).
- 8 rows: scaled estimate — pairs scale 32/128 of r32, excess ≈ 465 × 32/128 = 116 MB → 0.6 ms.
- 32 rows: 465 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = 2.3 ms.

Arithmetic is a floor (values the excess at peak bandwidth); the measured experts time is 14.67 ms, so the rest must come from overhead removal, not this entry.

## Verdict

1|# The swarm's shared documents, and the rules every agent keeps
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Part of the [muse-round skill](SKILL.md). [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|Every agent of the round reads this file. The documents below are how the swarm shares what it knows and how surucuonur follows the round while it runs, so keep them current as you work, not at the end.
6|
7|## The two phase folders
8|
9|| Folder | Phase | Holds |
10||---|---|---|
11|| `muse-spark/exploration/` | Exploration | the analysis: `README.md`, territory and inefficiency entries, `log.md` |
12|| `muse-spark/implementation/` | Implementation | the report: `README.md`, hypothesis entries, `log.md` |
13|
14|Kernels stay where the grader reads them: `muse-spark/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>/`.
15|
16|Each folder has three kinds of document:
17|
18|- **`README.md`.** The phase's document. Only the lead writes it, refreshing it and raising its version at every checkpoint. It opens with its version line and the tracker table below.
19|- **Entries.** One file per territory, inefficiency or hypothesis. The owner keeps it current, and other agents append notes.
20|- **`log.md`.** One line per event, from every agent, appended only.
21|
22|## Versions
23|
24|Every shared document carries a version number, so a reader knows which version they're looking at, and git holds every version.
25|
26|**Phase versions.** Each README opens with its version line:
27|
28|```markdown
29|**Version:** v5 · 2026-11-04T09:40Z · skill version 3
30|```
31|
32|- **Who raises it:** the lead, at every checkpoint, and each version is exactly one commit.
33|- **The commit:** its subject names the version, `Muse Spark: exploration v5: <what changed>`. `git log --grep 'exploration v5:'` finds it, and `git diff` between two such commits shows what changed.
34|- **The changelog:** the README ends with `## Versions`, one line per version, newest first, naming the entries that changed and their new versions:
35|
36|```markdown
37|- v5 · 2026-11-04T09:40Z · split quantized-kernels in two · changed: territory-quantized-kernels v4, ineff-quantized-kernels-2 v2
38|```
39|
40|**Entry versions.** Each entry's status block has a `Version` line, starting at 1:
41|- **Territory and inefficiency entries:** the owner raises it with every change to its own text. The verifier raises it when it writes the verdict.
42|- **Hypothesis entries:** the lead raises it at each checkpoint where the entry changed, builders' and the boundary agent's sections included.
43|- **Notes:** a note under `## From other agents` leaves the version alone. The owner raises it when folding the note in.
44|
45|## The README trackers
46|
47|Exploration, `exploration/README.md`:
48|
49|| Territory | Agent | Status | Inefficiencies | Updated |
50||---|---|---|---|---|
51|| `quantized-kernels` | `explorer-quantized-kernels` | exploring | `ineff-quantized-kernels-1` (confirmed), `-2` (open) | 2026-11-04 09:40Z |
52|
53|Implementation, `implementation/README.md`:
54|
55|| Hypothesis | Slot | Builders | Attempts: G1, G2, µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (compiled) | Status |
56||---|---|---|---|---|

58|
59|## Entries
60|
61|Each entry opens with a status block that its owner keeps current:
62|
63|```markdown
64|- **Owner:** explorer-quantized-kernels
65|- **Status:** exploring
66|- **Version:** 3
67|- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T09:40Z
68|- **Next:** read the 32-row dispatch of affine_gather_qmm
69|```
70|
71|Entries are named so that two agents never pick the same name:
72|- `exploration/territory-<territory>.md`
73|- `exploration/ineff-<territory>-<n>.md`, numbered by the explorer of that territory
74|- `implementation/hyp-<n>-<slug>.md`, numbered by the lead
75|
76|**Another agent's entry:** append under its `## From other agents` heading, starting with your name and the time. The owner's text stays as written, so two agents never overwrite each other. The owner reads these notes and folds in what holds.
77|
78|### Territory entry
79|
80|1. Status block (statuses: `exploring`, `done`).
81|2. **What it does** in the decode step, in a few lines.
82|3. **The checklist** below, filled in for each piece of code or table in the territory.
83|4. **Relations:** which territories feed it and which it feeds, with the data passed.
84|5. **Inefficiencies:** links to the entries this territory raised.
85|6. **Files read**, and what each one gave.
86|
87|### Inefficiency entry
88|
89|1. Status block. The statuses are `open`, `confirmed`, `refuted` and `superseded by <entry>`; only the verifier sets `confirmed` or `refuted`.
90|2. **Slot:** `routing`, `combine`, `experts`, or `outside the slots`.
91|3. **What happens:** what the code does, and where (file and lines).
92|4. **Cost** at 1, 8 and 32 rows: kernels × the fixed cost per kernel, bytes ÷ peak bandwidth, and the measured time with the table it comes from.
93|5. **Kind:** overhead-bound, bandwidth-bound or compute-bound, in the terms of `claude/GLOSSARY.md`.
94|6. **Spans:** the territories involved.
95|7. **Predicted saving** if removed, in µs per decode step at 1, 8 and 32 rows, with the arithmetic.
96|8. **Verdict**, written by the verifier: each claim checked, and the result.
97|
98|### Hypothesis entry
99|
100|1. Status block. The lead owns it; the statuses are `boundary`, `building`, `hardening`, `ready` and `dropped`.
101|2. **Inefficiency** it removes, and the slot.
102|3. **Boundary**, written by the boundary agent: what the solution must keep identical (see `boundary.md`).
103|4. **One section per builder:** its direction, its attempts (folder, predicted and measured µs per layer at 1, 8 and 32 rows, G1, G2), and what each attempt taught.
104|5. **Boundary checks** of the attempts that passed G2.
105|6. **Decision:** the best attempt and why. When the status is `ready`, it states what G3 should show.
106|
107|## The checklist
108|
109|Fill it in for each piece of code you inspect, so that no piece is judged without its neighbours:
110|
111|- **Callers:** who calls it, and with what shapes at 1, 8 and 32 rows.
112|- **Callees:** what it calls, down to the Metal kernel it launches.
113|- **Data:** each input and output with shape, dtype and layout. Where it is produced, and where it is consumed next.
114|- **Neighbours:** what runs just before and after it in the decode step, and what a replacement must keep identical.
115|- **Cost:** the kernels it launches, the bytes it reads and writes (weight bytes counted per read), and its measured time with the table the time comes from.
116|- **Invariants:** what correctness depends on: the G2 tolerances, the tie rule for the 4th and 5th expert, the bfloat16 rounding points.
117|
118|## The log
119|
120|Append one line per event with the shell, so lines from several agents never mix:
121|
122|```bash
123|printf '%s | %s | %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "explorer-quantized-kernels" "posted ineff-quantized-kernels-2: each weight byte read 4 times at 32 rows" >> muse-spark/exploration/log.md
124|```
125|
126|Log when you start, claim something, post or confirm an entry, change direction (what from, what to, and which entry made you), grade an attempt (with its verdict), and finish.
127|
128|## Adapting to the others' work
129|
130|Before every new piece of work, and after every post:
131|1. Read the phase README's tracker and the newest 30 lines of the phase log (`tail -n 30`).
132|2. Then change direction when:
133|   - **someone else covers it:** another entry already covers the same code or cause, so append to that entry instead of starting a second one;
134|   - **its premise fell:** the claim your work rests on was refuted;
135|   - **something pays more:** an open item in your territory or task predicts a larger saving than what you're on, and nobody owns it.
136|3. When you change direction, log it with the reason, and write it in your own entry's status block.
137|
138|Two claims on the same item go to the lead, who settles them.
139|
140|## Rules for every agent
141|
142|- **Writes go only to `muse-spark/`, in the files your role names.** Everything else in the worktree, and everything outside it, is read-only.
143|- **Only the lead commits.** Helpers never run `git add` or `git commit`.
144|- **The grader is the only GPU job.** Run it only as a builder, through the brief's command; it waits its turn when another run has the GPU. Load no model and start no other GPU work: the machine has 16 GB and slows down sharply when memory runs short.
145|- **Every number has a source:** a file and line, a table (path and row), a grader verdict (attempt folder), or arithmetic shown in full.
146|- **Credentials stay unread:** `.env` files, `~/.config/muse/` and any key store.
147|- **The API-stage kernels** in the history before the tag `agent-era` are from an earlier, removed stage (PROVENANCE.md) and stay unread.

An attempt another builder is still writing waits for its own commit. An entry that is mid-edit is committed as it stands, and finished in a later commit.
